Each is a row of the report (`symbol-font-character`), its code, how many, and what it was made, a summary's naming its table, since a dingbat font, Wingdings say, writes its characters there too, which would be made wrong: the report says each was taken as the Symbol font's. A separate agent's review raised it, with Wingdings' bullets and ticks (U+F0A7 ▪ made ♣, U+F0FC ✓ made ⎫), and found the summaries unreported. OpenStax's repositories here have no dingbat's: each of the ten there is the Symbol font's by its sense, and six reach a book:*Life, Liberty*'s two em dashes, in a letter home of 1945 ("ailments—a sprained right ankle"); *Introductory Statistics 2e*'s alpha ("Since α > p"); and a minus sign in a calculator screen's description ("a = −173.513363") in it, in *Statistics*, and in its Spanish edition, *Introducción a la estadística*. The other four, alphas, are in Try It solutions baking leaves out. In the 21 Connexions archive books here, 660 are in three: 658 in a Vietnamese book on solar energy, *Năng lượng mặt trời*, every one a Greek letter (τ 178 times, δ 77, ω 45) or a relation or operator (≤, ≈, ∑, ⊥, ⇒, and ÷, which it sets a range with, "(15÷30) km/s"), the Symbol font's by their sense; a minus sign in *Collaborative Statistics*; and in *Natural Sciences Grade 7*, 0x34 alone in a checklist's cell over its Yes and No columns, likely a dingbat's, made "4". The CNX suite's economics book has a paragraph with an alpha, a minus sign, and a dash, and a table's summary with the dash, which reaches the converted page's caption and the report, and `finish` is given an alt text's and a formula's; its checks fail under six mutations.

44. **A PDF's bookmarks go as deep as `pdf.toc_depth` says with no contents page too.** Rob, of the LibreTexts session's finding (Open questions): "Is this a bug in Pandoc? Can we work around it in a way that won't break when the bug is fixed?" Not by Pandoc's manual, which gives `toc-depth` as the "level of section to include in table of contents" and says nothing of bookmarks. But hyperref gives a heading a bookmark when its level is within LaTeX's `tocdepth` (its own `bookmarksdepth` unset), and Pandoc's template sets `tocdepth` only inside `$if(toc)$`, where it writes the contents, so a book whose `pdf.metadata` file says `toc: false` had the class's own depth, a subsection in the book class, and its bookmarks went a level deeper than `pdf.toc_depth` (item 35 had made the contents, and the bookmarks with them, as deep as the setting). `build-pdf.py` sets `tocdepth` at the head of `header-includes`, ahead of the author's own LaTeX, which can still set another; with a contents page the template sets it again, to the same. Were the template to set it outside `$if(toc)$`, it would set the same value, so the line would do nothing and break nothing. The PDF suite's preamble book has no contents page and a page with a section and a subsection, and its bookmarks are its pages and the section; the check fails with the line taken out (1 mutation).

45. **`build-pdf.py` run on its own: a relative `-d`, and a LaTeX book.** From PROJECT-NOTES' worth investigating; Rob, of each: "Fix it." With `-d book`, a folder given relative to where the build ran, and a `pdf.metadata` file, the build stopped ("Could not find metadata file"): Pandoc, which runs in the book's folder, was given the file's path relative to where the build ran. `metadata_file` gives it the whole path. And on a LaTeX book, `--latex-only` say, it wrote the default page and none of the book's colors, which `convert.py` passes in its environment (`BOOK_LATEX_LAYOUT` and `BOOK_LATEX_COLORS`), and LaTeX stops on a formula naming a color nothing defines (OpenIntro's). `latex_book` reads them as `convert.py` does when they aren't passed, from the masters `latex.main` chooses: `latexsource.chosen_masters`, which `convert.py`'s `latex_masters` now uses too, its messages the same, and `latexsource.book_page`, which `prepare` uses, each color statement once, as `convert.py` passes them. A book that isn't LaTeX has no master, as `convert.py` finds none, and gets the default page. The PDF suite's preamble book is built again by hand, from the folder above it with `-d` relative; the LaTeX suite's customized book, OpenIntro's shapes, with `--latex-only` and none of `convert.py`'s environment, keeps its 11pt type, its margins, and a color of its own; the checks fail under four mutations, one of them a binder taken for a master, which the LaTeX suite's binder check catches through the code the two now share.

46. **The page for WCAG 1.4.8 (AAA) counts spacing from the type's size.** Rob, of the two readings (item 40): "It sounds like 1.5 times the type's size is defensible, so go with that." W3C's technique C21, one of the criterion's sufficient techniques, which W3C says meet it, measures space-and-a-half from the type's size (CSS's `line-height: 150%`), where W3C's explanation of the criterion measures it from single spacing, "the default spacing for the font", 1.2 times the type's size in LaTeX; only the criterion's own words are normative, and they don't say. The page now: 13.5-point type as before; lines 1.5 times the type's size apart, the default's own (`linestretch: 1.25`); paragraphs 2.5 times it apart, top to top (`\setlength{\parskip}{1em plus 2pt}`); and footnotes' and captions' lines 1.5 times their type's size (`\SetSinglespace{1.25}`). *Introduction to Sociology 3e* is 1,208 pages on it, about 24 percent longer than the default's 975, where the other reading's 1,408 are 44 percent, each built from the same pages, unpacked with item 41's boxes (2026-10-21); the configuration page gives that reading's three lines. The PDF suite's AAA book: lines 1.5 times its 13.45 points apart; the least space between paragraphs, over the pages, within half a point of 2.5 times it, since a full page's gaps are stretched to fill it (`\flushbottom`); and a footnote's and a caption's lines 1.5 times their type's size. Three mutations, each caught, the paragraphs' at 1.2em only once the check allowed half a point either way, where it had allowed three over.

47. **An OpenStax book's PDF is set in its design's face, at 12 points.** Rob, of OpenStax's typefaces (TextbookImprover observations): "Let's follow your plan for adopting the OpenStax typefaces selectively, sticking to 12 pt." The plan: the text faces, which are larger at a given size than Latin Modern and sturdier, and not the heading faces, three of which draw a capital I and a small l alike. `cnx.project`'s `DESIGNS` names each design's face and its styles, as ce-styles' typography settings (`baseFont`) and each style's `book.scss` give them: cosmos IBM Plex Serif (12 styles), carnival IBM Plex Sans (18, *Organic Chemistry* in its design's second face, Plex Serif), and cardboard and corn Noto Sans (16 and 8); `ap-history` and `otto-book`, which have no design there, keep Latin Modern, and a check keeps every style a recipe bakes in a design or in that list. The unpacker writes the face's lines into the book's `pdf-layout.yaml` (`mainfont`), under a comment saying what they do, unless the file names a face or a math font already, so a copy someone edited keeps theirs; the headings, which Pandoc's template sets in the text's face, are its bold. The face is named by its four files (`mainfont: NotoSans`, and in `mainfontoptions` `Extension=.ttf`, `UprightFont=*-Regular`, `BoldFont=*-Bold`, `ItalicFont=*-Italic`, and `BoldItalicFont=*-BoldItalic`), so a file that isn't installed stops the build, which names it: named by its family, Noto Sans was matched by Noto Sans Medium, its bold by ExtraBold, and the build went on without a word, where TeX Live was Debian's, whose `noto` has no Regular, Bold, or Italic, and `fonts-noto-core`, which has them, wasn't installed, as a separate agent's review found with a font database of its own. A Plex Serif book's formulas are in IBM Plex Math (`mathfont: IBMPlexMath-Regular.otf`), whose letters are Plex Serif's. A Plex Sans book's stay in Latin Modern Math, IBM Plex having no math font with Plex Sans's letters, and so do a Noto Sans book's, its line for Noto Sans Math commented out: the Noto Sans Math of Debian's and Ubuntu's `fonts-noto-core` (2.001, in Ubuntu 24.04 through 26.10) has no MATH table, the measurements unicode-math sets a formula by, and given it, unicode-math sets formulas in Latin Modern Math; notofonts' 3.000 has one, and TeX Live has no OpenType Noto Sans Math. It needed two things of the PDF target first. A face a metadata file named got no fallback fonts (`build-pdf.py` gave them only to the families it left at Latin Modern), and Noto Sans lacks the minus sign and most of mathematics' symbols (≤, ≠, ≈, →, ∞, √, ∑, ∫), and IBM Plex ⇒ and the circled letters and digits (ⓐ, ①), so each was left out of the PDF; a named face gets them now, unless the file gives its own (`mainfontfallback` and the rest), and the text's face is set again for babel, whose copy of it Pandoc's template sets the text in when a book has a language (PANDOC-NOTES), and which `\setmainfont` doesn't reach. And a face that isn't installed stops LaTeX, which the run now says, naming the face and where an OpenStax book's come from (TeX Live's `plex` and `noto`, or on Debian and Ubuntu `fonts-noto-core`, which their TeX Live recommends). Measured (2026-10-20), each unpacked and built by `convert.py`, the output check and veraPDF on: *Introduction to Sociology 3e*, whole, is 1,032 pages in Plex Serif and 975 in Latin Modern, built beside it, and nothing is found in either; *Principles of Economics 3e*'s chapter 5 is 39 pages in Plex Serif and Plex Math, and *Chemistry 2e*'s chapter 3 65 in Plex Sans, one display formula 87 points too wide, nothing found in either; and *College Algebra 2e*'s chapter 1 is 136 pages in Noto Sans and 128 in Latin Modern, with 28 lines too wide, the widest by 224 points, where Latin Modern has 14, by 136, and veraPDF fails both on two glyphs of LaTeX's `line10` font, which the cancel package's strokes are drawn with (Open questions). Checked in the CNX suite (a style of each design, named by its files, *Organic Chemistry*'s face, a style with no design, an edited default given the face and one naming its own keeping it, and the converted book's LaTeX setting the face by its files for fontspec and babel, with the fallbacks, and Plex Math for formulas), the PDF suite (the fancy book in Plex Serif, named by its files, its ⇒ drawn), and the LaTeX suite (a missing face named across fontspec's lines); twelve mutations, each caught.

48. **A formula's term struck out is drawn as paths.** Rob, of the `line10` font (Open questions): "Yes, fix the strike-through issue." Pandoc's template loads the cancel package for a formula that names `\cancel`, `\bcancel`, or `\xcancel` (PANDOC-NOTES), which texmath writes for MathML's diagonal strikes, as OpenStax's math books have them, and a deck's template does the same; cancel draws each stroke with picture mode's `\line`, and `\cancelto`'s arrow with `\vector`, glyphs of LaTeX's `line10` font, whose map to Unicode in the PDF has only a space, and veraPDF failed *College Algebra 2e*'s first chapter on two of them (8.4.5.8, in PDF/UA-2 and both WTPDF profiles), in Noto Sans and in Latin Modern alike. pict2e draws picture mode's lines and arrows as paths, with no font. cancel, given pict2e, asks for LaTeX's own commands (`\OriginalPictureCmds`), its comment saying pict2e's have no bounding box, which pict2e's `\line` has now. `latexbuild.CANCEL_STROKES`, which a book's PDF and a deck's read in `PDF_MACROS` and `texremediate.tag` adds to the tagged copy of a LaTeX book that loads cancel, loads pict2e where cancel is loaded, at the end of the preamble (the `begindocument/before` hook, after any pict2e a book or a deck loads with options of its own), and makes `\OriginalPictureCmds` nothing, so cancel draws with pict2e's. pict2e has drawing commands of its own, `\arc`, `\Line`, `\polygon`, `\moveto`, and nineteen more, and loaded so late, as a separate review of the change found when it loaded pict2e for every PDF, it replaced a book's own `\arc`, on which LaTeX then stopped ("Missing number"), and stopped LaTeX on a book's own `\circlearc` and on a `\newcommand` of `\Line` in a book's text ("already defined"; measured on test pages). So those names are set aside before pict2e loads and, at `\begin{document}`, given back as the book had them or taken away, but for `\maxovalrad`, which pict2e's `\oval` reads, and the trig package's `\UseSin` and the rest, which pict2e loads and uses, a book's own of which still stops LaTeX (`\maxovalrad`) or is replaced (`\UseSin`), names a book is unlikely to have; a book that loads pict2e itself keeps all of it; and a PDF with no cancel loads no pict2e at all. A tagged copy made from such a copy, as a `source` target's laid over a book's folder is, gets it once, since its constant twice stops LaTeX ("already defined"). Measured on a page of `\cancel`, `\bcancel`, `\xcancel`, and `\cancelto`, in text, in a script, and displayed, built tagged with and without it and rendered at 300 dpi: each stroke where it was, the pixels that differ (3,739 of 8.4 million) its edges, no `line10` font, and veraPDF's 8.4.5.8 gone; and on pages with a book's own `\arc`, a `\newcommand` of `\Line` in the text, and a book's own pict2e: each the book's. Built again with it, *College Algebra 2e*'s first chapter has its 136 pages in Noto Sans and 128 in Latin Modern, its 24 strokes drawn as paths, each where it was (rendered at 150 dpi, Noto Sans's pages differ only around the strokes), and no `line10` font; veraPDF's three findings are gone from each, and the output check's six others and its lines too wide, 28 and 14, are as they were. Checked in the PDF suite's notes book (a fraction's terms struck out, `\bcancel`, and `\xcancel`: five lines on their page, and no `line10` glyph, tagged or not; and an `\arc` the book defines in its text, its own), the decks suite (a deck with two terms struck out and an `\xcancel`: four lines, no `line10` glyph), and the LaTeX suite (a LaTeX book that loads cancel and defines `\arc` in its preamble: two lines in its PDF from its own LaTeX and from its pages, no `line10` glyph, its `\arc` its own, and the run's report saying so; a tagged copy of a book that strikes a term out, its report, and the copy made again from itself, which builds, its own `\cbezier` its own; a book that loads pict2e itself, its `\cbezier` drawing; and a document with no cancel, no pict2e). Thirteen mutations, each caught: `CANCEL_STROKES` left out of `PDF_MACROS` (by the PDF suite and the decks suite), out of a deck's macros alone, and out of a LaTeX book's copy; cancel still asking for LaTeX's own commands; pict2e's names neither set aside nor given back; a book's own not set aside (by the LaTeX suite, whose book defines `\arc` before `\begin{document}`); pict2e's own of a name the book hadn't left in place; `\cbezier` left off the names; pict2e loaded with no cancel; a book's own pict2e's names set aside too; the copy made from a copy given it again; and each report leaving it out, the tagged copy's and the PDF target's. veraPDF alone wouldn't have caught the first: with the strokes drawn in `line10`, it passed the notes book and the deck, where it failed *College Algebra*'s chapter and the test page on two glyphs each; why it reports some of the font's glyphs and not others wasn't found. 50. **A table or a formula too wide for its line is fitted to it, in a PDF.** Rob, of the lines too wide (Open questions): "what is the cleanest way to ensure that everything stays on the 'paper'?", and "can we simply substitute smaller fonts for just the too-wide tables or displayed equations? Maybe try narrowing the spaces first and then going to a smaller font if that's not enough?" So it's done, with LaTeX telling which run over, since a count ahead of it can't: `pdf-target.lua`'s, 70 characters to a line of 10-point type, had set a table whose longest words don't fit a line in `\small` or `\footnotesize`, the first they fit in by the count, which left *Introductory Business Statistics 2e*'s F tables up to 172 points too wide in `\footnotesize`, in 12-point Noto Sans, and set the notes book's table of two long words smaller, though it fits. `pdf-target.lua` numbers each table not in a table's cell, each display formula the writer sets in `\[ \]`, and each formula in text that is an environment, as a worked example's steps are an array, each in a group (`\OERFitTable`, `\OERFitFormula`), and `latexbuild.FIT_MACROS`, in `PDF_MACROS`, measures each as LaTeX sets it: a table by the widths longtable records for its columns (`\LT@save@row`) and, where its columns wrap, by the longest piece TeX can't break of each line of its cells against its column (`post_linebreak_filter`); a formula by what TeX makes of it (`post_mlist_to_hlist_filter`). One too wide is fitted on the next run, as Pandoc runs LaTeX again: its spaces narrowed (a table's columns half an em apart, where they were 12 points; a formula's `\qquad` a quad, an `\mspace` wider than a quad a quad, and an array's columns 0.4 as far apart), and where that's not enough its type set smaller, as much as it takes but to three quarters of its size at least, a table whose columns wrap given columns as wide as its words need. A table or a display formula fitted is centered on the page, its `\LTleft` and `\LTright`, or its `\displayindent` and `\displaywidth`, reaching into both margins, so one still too wide runs into both alike, and one that would come within a quarter inch of the paper's edge even at three quarters is set smaller still, to half its size at least; a formula in text still too wide runs into the margin on its right. A numbered display (`\tag`, as `equation()` writes a book's number), `e` to `pdf-target.lua`, isn't centered: centered, its number was set at the end of a line as wide as the margins allow, past the text's edge; TeX sets the number beside the formula, squeezing its spaces if it must, or on a line of its own. A display under the `fleqn` class option isn't fitted, fleqn setting it in a box as wide as the line, a margin from its left end. On a page of two columns a fit has no margin to run into, since the margin there is the other column, so a formula is set smaller to fit its column, to half its size at least, and what's still too wide runs past it, into the space between the columns or across the other, and is warned of as too wide for its column, not for the paper; a fit made on the second run can leave a formula a few points past its column, a smaller design being wider for its size (below). A book in two columns can't have a table, since longtable stops there, but for a table of the class `float`, which the writer sets as a `tabular` in a `table` float (PANDOC-NOTES), and which isn't fitted: a table is measured by the widths longtable records, and those a floating table's group found were the last longtable's, so that the fit book's floating table, after one too wide for the paper at half its type, was fitted to them and warned of as too wide for the paper, its columns 3 points apart, where they're 12. A display's smaller type keeps the text's line spacing: TeX sets the lines of the paragraph before it as it begins, inside the fit's group, and set with the smaller spacing too they were closer together. A layout table's caption, a paragraph before it, is before the group, in the text's type. A table whose columns wrap, once fitted, isn't hyphenated: in the fit book's table of 22 columns, set at 51 percent, the 6-point design, wider for its size than the 7-point the fit was measured in, left the corner's "Twentytwo" a point wider than its column, and TeX broke it ("Twen-tytwo"), where now it runs a point into the space beside the column. A wrapping table whose spaces between its columns alone fill its line, as a table of 45 columns whose widths are given does on the default page, the writer giving its columns less than no width (PANDOC-NOTES), was left as it was, its numbers printed over one another, and named only among the lines too wide, 48 of its lines; its spaces are narrowed on the first run now, which gives its columns some width, and it's fitted on the second, the fit book's at 61 percent. A wrapping table's columns are worked out with the spaces between them at the size it's set in: counted at the size the run before had, a table set larger on the second run than on the first, as *Introductory Business Statistics 2e*'s F tables are, longtable's first widths under the head across their columns having made them too small, had narrower columns than counted, and in seven of them "denominator" ran 1.6 to 3.4 points past its column (Table A7 at 98.8 percent, where it's at 93.5 now). And a cell's line's longest piece leaves out a box as wide as the line, a head cell's minipage, which had counted every head cell as filling its column. Smaller type isn't proportionally narrower, measured: Latin Modern Roman, the default face, has designs for sizes from 5 to 17 points, each wider for its size than the next larger, 2.2 percent from 12 points to 10, 2.8 from 10 to 9, 3.3 from 9 to 8, and 6.7 from 8 to 7; and unicode-math sets math of 10 points or less, in 12-point type, in its font's forms for subscripts (ssty), 13 percent wider for their size, and of 7 or less in the second level's forms, 38 percent wider, and in 10-point type math of 8 or less in the first. So whatever is too wide is fitted on LaTeX's first run, a formula's spaces narrowed and its type set smaller at once, and on the second each fit is measured again and fitted again where it's off its line by more than 4 percent of it, too wide or too narrow, more than a design's step, or, for a formula in text or a numbered display, which nothing centers, too wide at all. The notes book's table of numbers, in 10-point type, fitted at 86 percent (8.57 points, the 9-point design), is 1.2 points too wide, centered; fitted again, it was at 84 percent (the 8-point design) and 2.7 too wide. And longtable gets some first runs' widths wrong: where a table's head is one row, a cell across columns, it gives the last of those columns the cell's whole width (the F tables' "Degrees of freedom in the numerator", Table A1's last column 621 points), so that they were 816 points too wide on the first run and 254 on the second, which the second run's fit sets right. Nothing is fitted after the second run: fitted on the third as well, *College Algebra 2e*'s first chapter ended its fourth with "Label(s) may have changed", the pages of LaTeX's last run not those of the run its labels, the contents' page numbers among them, were read from. `pdf-target.lua`'s count leaves a table of 25 columns or more in the columns the writer gives one without widths: it had shared out a line with no room left in it, and the writer gave a table of 45 columns of numbers columns of less than no width, its numbers printed over one another (PANDOC-NOTES). The build says what it fitted, by narrowing and in smaller type, names what's still wider than its line, centered, and warns of what's too wide for the paper even in smaller type, or for its column on a page of two, with the smallest size it's in (`latexbuild.fit_report`); a formula still too wide, but a display centered within the margins, is among the lines too wide as well, LaTeX's overfull boxes. A deck's PDF, which `pdf-target.lua` and `PDF_MACROS` build too, fits a slide's table or formula the same way, where the decks suite's slide of a table of twelve columns ran 147 points off it and its formula 234, built with `main`'s code; and the `latex` target's LaTeX carries the marks, which `latexsource.fit_marks` takes out when it's read back as a LaTeX source, since Pandoc's reader expanded them as the preamble defines them and stopped ("unexpected ()"). The `.aux` file counts LaTeX's runs once something is fitted, and as the second from the second on, so that it stops changing: counted as the run, and with nothing fitted too, it changed on every run, so that latexmk stopped the `latex` target's build at its most runs, five, and a deck's build warned that its cross-references were still changing, as each commit's suites, run on the series before delivery, found. And it keeps a digest of each of the book's own `.tex` files LaTeX reads (by a path from its folder, not TeX's own): the main file, each it reads lines of once the fitting's macros are in, a chapter or a file read with TeX's own `\input`, and each read with `\input{}` before them, as a book's header-includes are, which LaTeX's list of files has: a book edited and built again beside the files of an earlier build, as the `latex` target is, had the earlier fits applied by their numbers to what now had them, and nothing new fitted, the count saying no more runs were to fit. A mark of what was numbered, each one's kind, columns, and line, missed what changed without moving, a formula edited on its own line, which kept its old fit, or a master given wider margins, where a formula that had fit was too wide and wasn't fitted; and a digest of only the files LaTeX's own `\input{}` and `\include` read after the fitting's macros missed one input before them and one read with TeX's own `\input`. Now, before any fit is set, a file whose digest differs has the fitting start again. Measured (2026-10-21 and 22), each book's LaTeX run four times as Pandoc runs it, and built whole by `build-pdf.py`, the output check and veraPDF after: *College Algebra 2e*'s first chapter, in Noto Sans, had 28 formulas too wide, the widest by 224 points; 11 fit with their spaces narrowed and 17 in smaller type, two of those, worked examples' steps in text, still too wide at three quarters of their size, by 36 points and by 0.6, so the build names one line too wide where it named 28, and the output check finds what it did (six `pdf-table-header-is-formula`). *Introductory Business Statistics 2e*'s appendix A had 40 lines too wide, the widest by 172 points; its 13 tables too wide are fitted, 5 with their spaces narrowed and 8 in smaller type, Table A1 the smallest, at 83 percent, none of them still wider than the text; no line is too wide, and the output check finds nothing. Checked in the PDF suite's fit book, on the default page (24 checks: a table that narrowed spaces fit, one in smaller type, one left 2 percent too wide by the 9-point design and centered, not fitted again, one centered at three quarters of its type, one set smaller still to stay on the paper, one too wide for the paper at half, its 45 columns as the writer sets them, warned of, a floating table after it in the text's type and spacing, one whose head is a cell across its columns, fitted again on the second run in the text's type and spacing, one of formulas fitted again on the second run, one whose columns wrap, fitted with its spaces narrowed in the text's type, Table A7's second-run fit worked out by `texlua` from its measures, one whose columns' widths are given, a word too long for its column, a layout table, its caption in the text's type, one of 45 columns whose widths are given, narrowed and then fitted, and one of 22 columns, its corner wrapping, kept on the paper with its words whole; display formulas likewise, one in a paragraph whose lines before it keep their spacing, one whose spaces narrowed fit it, one fitted again on the second run, one centered, and a numbered one, its number at its line's end; a worked example's steps fitted again on the second run; nothing fitted on a third run; and the build's report) and its book in two columns under `fleqn` (3 checks: a display left as fleqn sets it, steps set smaller for their column, and the warning of what's too wide for its column), the notes book's two tables, and the untagged book's formula, too wide now for the paper even at half its type and named still; in the decks suite (a slide's table and formula fitted inside its edges, the deck's runs settling, and a deck with nothing to fit settling in two runs, as before); and in the LaTeX suite (the `latex` target's long sum marked, its build by latexmk settling with it fitted, built again after an edit with each formula fitted by its own measure, and after one in place with nothing fitted, and the target read back; and a document of LaTeX's own whose file input before the fitting's macros, and whose file read with TeX's own `\input`, each edited, has the fitting start again); forty mutations, each caught.

51. **A table's notes on its rows are no bands, and leave it no header column.** Rob, of *Prealgebra 2e*'s Table 3.1 (Open questions): "can we detect these cases and give them the right guess up front?" A row one cell across that ends as a sentence does, with a full stop, a question mark, or an exclamation mark, any closing quotation marks or brackets after it, right after a row of the table's cells, in a table that ends with such a row, is a note on the rows above it, not a band over the rows below (`tablecensus.note_rows`). The split doesn't cut the table there, as it doesn't at its foot's rows, and the guess (`explain`) gives a table with a note before its last row no header column, since no cell of a note's row could head it, and a writer cuts a cell across a body's row-head columns (PANDOC-NOTES): `both` is `first-row`; `first-column` is `first-row` where the source marks a header row (`head_rows`: a `<thead>`, a Word table's first row its table look formats, a row marked to repeat) and `none` where nothing does; and `unknown` is `none` where nothing does, but for a table whose header row is below a data row, which stays `unknown`, as one with a marked head does, Word's look making a head of any table. A part's guess, between bands, goes the same way (`guess_table`), and the reason leaves out the clause `table-headers.py` reads as a summary row's, since a summary row's empty label has no column to keep it. A table that opens with such a sentence has no notes, a table of bands (a self-test closed by its total's line, "Add up your scores for your total."), and a line at a table's foot that says where it comes from (`ATTRIBUTION`: "Adapted from …", "Source: …") is no note, nor what makes a table end with one, nor a row a note comes before: a table closed by a note and then its source's line keeps its header column, as it would without the line. Of the 15,935 tables the census was run on, the 12,992 the unpacker writes for the books cloned here and the Word corpus's 2,943, six are guessed otherwise: Table 3.1 (`first-column`, split at its first note) and Table 3.4 (`unknown`, split at its first note), each `none` and whole; their copies in chapter 3's Key Concepts and a table of *Intermediate Algebra 2e*'s section 2.1, all three layout tables; and *Clinical Nursing Skills*' steps in two columns in 8.3, a step across both first and last, `first-row` still and no longer split at its first step. Measured by leaving each out, against the rule as it is, two of its conditions keep tables as they were: a row of cells before the note, 20 (16 of them *Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness*' inquiry organizers, sentences under a title), and the table's ending with one, 33 (28 of them worked examples' steps in the algebra books, layout tables); `unknown` made `none` changes 3, Table 3.4, its copy, and *Intermediate Algebra 2e*'s; and the guards for a table that opens with a sentence, an attribution, and a marked header row change none of the 15,935, the cases they're for made up to test the rule, a self-test closed by its total's line or by its source among them. Three tests of a sentence's form, no parentheses round it, three words or more, and not in title case, changed none of the 15,935, so the rule hasn't them. The row Rob declared for Table 3.1, `none`, says what the guess says now. Checked in the census suite (Table 3.1's shape and 3.4's, the steps, a table formatting marks both, a header row Word's table look formats, a header row below a data row, a table no rule recognizes with Word's look, a note within a part between bands, a summary row's empty label, a self-test, plain, cited at its foot, closed by its total's line, and with a header row and its source, a worked example's steps with a sentence across them, an organizer, labels in a table that ends with a note, and a note in the last row alone, with its source's line after it too); thirteen mutations, each caught.

52. **A worked example's steps written as one formula are a table whose reasons wrap.** Rob, of the steps still too wide at three quarters of their size (Open questions): "if we can fix something like the 'step tables' by wrapping the comments/instructions in their column, then that is a better solution for those. Go ahead with that." The emitter makes such a formula a layout table, class `formula-steps`, as the dev-math books' steps are (`steptables.formula_steps`): an `mtable` and nothing else, through what only groups, of rows of cells and nothing else, of two columns or more, but those empty in every row; its first or last column words, each of its cells that holds anything opening with text (an `mtext`, after any space) that holds a word, and one of them two words or more, a word being three letters or more, small after the first, so that a chemical formula's symbols aren't words (NaCl, KBr); math beside them (an `mi`, `mn`, or `mo` outside text); no column between the first and the last with two words in a cell; and not an equation's side written in words beside its relation ("Total damage = …", the economics books' way), a table of values, three columns of math or more, none a relation's, under a column of their names (*Elementary Algebra 2e*'s "Integer | −2 | −1 | 0 …"), or a formula with lines between its rows or columns, a labeled row, or a cell across columns or rows, which the table wouldn't span. Words the source broke over lines, a table of one column each of whose rows opens with text, are one cell's words ("Commutative and associative" over "properties of multiplication", *College Algebra 2e*'s 1.2). Lines labeled in words written as one formula are so too, as *Chemistry 2e* labels a cell's half-reactions ("oxidation half-reaction:"). It's a table where a table can stand, in a paragraph, a list item, or a division, an unnumbered equation's too; not in a table's cell, where a PDF's longtable can't be set, a footnote, a caption, a heading, or a numbered equation. Each cell of math is a formula of its own, in display style where the `mtable` set its cells so (which Pandoc's reader drops, PANDOC-NOTES, so every output sets them in text style, as it set the `mtable`'s), each column aligned as the `mtable` aligned its first cell holding anything (the HTML reader takes a column's alignment from the first row, PANDOC-NOTES), and the space that set it apart from the words beside it, an `mspace` of 1em to 13.5em in *College Algebra 2e*'s first chapter (2em the commonest, 76 times), or an empty text or an operator of a no-break space beside one, left to the table's columns; each cell of words is text, left aligned, its no-break spaces spaces a line can break at, bold or italic where it's set so, its math formulas, and the punctuation an `mo` that ends a run of math is text. A line break right before or after such a table goes, as a solution's lettered parts break the line between the letter and the formula. The run counts the tables. In the 42 of OpenStax's repositories here, 852 in 18 books, lines labeled in words among them (*Chemistry 2e*'s half-reactions, *Calculus Volume 3*'s "Normal vector:"): *Algebra and Trigonometry 2e*'s 197, *College Algebra with Corequisite Support 2e*'s 165, *College Algebra 2e*'s 160, *Precalculus 2e*'s 142, *Elementary Algebra 2e*'s 43, *Intermediate Algebra 2e*'s 35, *Calculus* Volume 1's 30, Volume 2's 29, and Volume 3's 17, *Prealgebra 2e*'s 11, *Chemistry: Atoms First 2e*'s 8 and *Chemistry 2e*'s 7, *Fizyka dla szkół wyższych* Volume 1's 2 and Volume 3's 1, *University Physics* Volume 1's 2 and Volume 3's 1, and *Algebra 1*'s and *Microbiology*'s one each (each book unpacked with the run's count). In a PDF, where LaTeX doesn't lay it out by its own measure (item 56), `pdf-target.lua` sets such a table at its own width where the line has room for it, and where it hasn't, each column of math as wide as its widest formula and a tenth more (`MATH_ROOM`), the words wrapping in what's left of the line, no narrower than their longest word or the widest formula among them and a tenth more, since it doesn't break either; where the formulas and the longest words together are wider than the line, the words are as wide as their longest and the formulas share what's left by their counts, and only steps whose longest words alone fill the line are set as any other table (`steps_widths`). Seven of *College Algebra 2e*'s first chapter's 51 tables of steps share so; set as other tables are, six of those seven would be set in smaller type to fit their formulas to their columns, and shared so, three are. A formula in such a table doesn't break over lines: `Table` sets `\binoppenalty` and `\relpenalty` to 10000 in the table's group, since TeX breaks a formula in text after an operator or a relation and FIT_MACROS measures a column by the longest piece TeX can't break, so that a formula wider than its column is fitted, not broken, as without them one of the steps of Example 6 (e), in section 1.1, would be. Pandoc's writer draws a rule above such a table and one below (`\toprule`, `\bottomrule`), as it does every table, where the formula had none. It counts a formula's width with `formula_width`, closer than `formula_length`, which counts a fraction's two parts one after the other and space around every operator, a script's and a formula's first: measured against LaTeX, each of the 301 step formulas in *College Algebra 2e*'s first chapter set in a box in Latin Modern Math at 12 points, `formula_length` counted them at 1.76 times their width (the median; 2.38 at the ninetieth percentile, and 4.09 the most, fractions), `formula_width` at 1.23 (1.27 at the ninetieth percentile, none under 0.93), an operator or a relation a command names, as `\leq`, as wide as `=`, but a dot, a function's name, as `\sin`, by its letters and one more for the space TeX sets beside it, where it had counted it one character, as `formula_length` does (`\sin x \cos x \tan x \cot x \sin y`, 129 points wide as LaTeX sets it in Latin Modern at 12 points, 22 of the filter's characters, 70 to a line of 10-point type, was counted 10, and is 25 now), but no space before an opening delimiter, where TeX sets none (`\ln(x)`, 4.4 characters wide, was counted 6, and is 5), though one before `\left(`, which makes a group TeX sets apart (`\log\left( x \right)` is 2 points wider than `\log(x)` at 12 points); limits set under something, as `\underset` and `\lim\limits` set them, as wide as the wider of the two, where it had counted them beside it, and a relation so set, as `\overset{?}{=}`, as a relation, which amsmath makes it; and an escaped symbol, as `\{`, and a text's spaces counted too, but not a space in `\mathrm`, where TeX sets none. With `formula_length`'s count, the chapter's steps that fit their line were set across it, their words wrapped, and a formula broke over its column's lines. The tenth more is the book's face's: Pandoc's template scales Latin Modern Math to the height of the text's small letters (`Scale=MatchLowercase`), and Noto Sans's are 24 percent taller than Latin Modern's (each of the 301 measured in both), so `formula_width` counts them at 0.90 of their width in the book's PDF, the median of the 205 that aren't an equals sign alone (0.81 at the tenth percentile, 0.75 the least; 0.99 with the 96 that are, which the count takes about right). The counts give a worked example's steps a blank as three underscores now too (item 57's last open one). FIT_MACROS' measures leave out the kerns a blank drawn at two thirds overlaps by, which they meet in a cell's lines and a reason's paragraph, the blank's drawing running before them: in a cell, the blank is three underscores to the measure, and in a reason's width, whole (Joinlong, Wholereason). 73. **A sidecar Excel saved as plain "CSV" is rewritten as UTF-8.** Rob (2026-10-25): "if I understand correctly, this is a breaking change and old sidecars will no longer work until they are updated to use UTF-8. Is that right? Can we detect and automatically rewrite sidecars that are in the old format so there is an easy upgrade path for users with old sidecars?" For a sidecar it isn't, measured on a one-page book with `image-alt.csv` and `table-captions.csv`: one in UTF-8, with the mark or without it, reads the same on d7306eb, before item 67's patch, as on f7969c2, after it; and one Excel saved as plain "CSV", in Windows-1252, never worked. On d7306eb each character outside ASCII was a U+FFFD in the page's alt text and caption ("Caf&#xFFFD; &#xFFFD; a r&#xFFFD;sum&#xFFFD;&#xFFFD;s"), and then the run stopped with a traceback, in `unreviewed_rows`; on f7969c2 it stops before converting, naming the line (item 69's check). What changed for a person's files is the reports' mark, which a script reading a report as `utf-8` finds before the first column's name, as the changelog's Breaking entry says, and it says now that sidecars need no change. So such a sidecar is rewritten now, by the run before anything is converted and by `table-headers.py`, `split-pages.py`, `util/remediate.py`, `util/round-trip-decks.py`, and `util/shortdoi.py` before they read it, `shortdoi.py --dry-run` reading it so and writing nothing (`sidecars.read_code_page` and `rewrite_as_utf8`, into which `sidecars.not_utf8` is folded). Its lines that aren't UTF-8 are read in Windows-1252 or in Mac OS Roman, the code pages Windows Excel's and Excel for Mac's plain "CSV" use in the US and Western Europe, as others report them (Donat Studios' "CSV: An Encoding Nightmare", 2016 to 2022; not tried here, where there's no Excel), whichever reads them with fewer characters misplaced (`sidecars.misplaced`): a sign or a letter where a misread one sits and text's seldom does, such as a Latin capital after a small letter ("donÕt" is "don’t" read in the wrong one) or between capitals before a small one ("OÕNeill"), a small letter before a capital ("ìHello"), a Latin letter between digits ("1990ñ2000"), a letter that can only be a misread sign standing alone ("a Ð b" for an en dash), ä after a number ("5 ä" for "5 ‰"), a third letter outside ASCII in a row (Cyrillic read as Latin), a mark between letters ("M‰rz"), a spacing accent ("¯ 25 mm" for "Ø 25 mm"), a superscript after a space, or ¹ between a digit and a letter ("p ² 0.05" for "p ≤ 0.05", "2¹r" for "2πr"), and ¡ with no ! after it ("100 ¡C" for "100 °C"), the five characters both read alike counting for nothing (M±SD). Where they have as many, the line ends decide, a CR alone Mac OS Roman's, as Excel 2011 for Mac saved them, and CR LF Windows-1252's, Excel 2016 for Mac ending lines as Windows does, as a Microsoft Q&A thread of 2016-11-30 reports. A line that is UTF-8, as a report's rows appended to the sidecar are, is kept as it is, and shown in the warning when it holds a character outside ASCII, since a line in the code page can happen to be UTF-8 ("Gauß’s" in Windows-1252 is UTF-8's "Gauߒs", "20 Å²" its "20 Ų", and "jusqu’à" in Mac OS Roman its "jusquՈ"); a file that's UTF-8 throughout isn't rewritten at all. The file as it was is kept beside it (`image-alt.csv.windows-1252` or `.mac-roman`, then `.2` and on), never written over; the new one is written beside it and moved into its place (`sidecars._replace`), its owner and mode kept, so a write that fails leaves it as it was, with no copy beside it; and the run warns, showing ten of the lines read in the code page and ten of those kept as UTF-8, a character that shows as nothing by its number (`<U+00A0>`). A file whose lines, two of them or more, all read with a character misplaced in each code page stops the run instead, saying how each reads them, and so do one with a byte Windows-1252 has no character for whose lines all read with one misplaced in Mac OS Roman, a control character, UTF-16, as Excel's "Unicode Text" saves a file, a read-only file, and on Windows one Excel has open. Measured on 58 lines written here to read like alt text and captions, in English with curly quotes, dashes, and signs, and in French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Danish, and Swedish, each saved alone in each code page: Windows-1252's 58 read right, and Mac OS Roman's 55 it can hold with a CR alone; with CR LF, 48 of the 55, the other 7 read as Windows-1252, their characters as plausible there ("señor" as "se–or", "schön" as "schšn", "Chloë’s" as "Chlo‘Õs", "1º" as "1¼", "« Bonjour »" as "Ç Bonjour È"). All in one file read right in each code page with each line end, and none stopped. On the reviewers' 553 lines (item 74), each alone: Windows-1252's 445 of 457 read right, 5 are UTF-8 by chance, read so and not rewritten ("JOSÉ’S FARM" is UTF-8's "JOSɒS FARM"), and 7 read as Mac OS Roman, a letter's name ("la letra Ñ"), a superscript after a space ("¹H NMR"), Portuguese's "Exmª", and Norwegian's "HiØs" among them; Mac OS Roman's 454 of 461 with a CR alone, those but the superscript missed, "ÅÄÖ åäö" stopping, and "L’école" UTF-8 by chance, and 319 of 461 with CR LF. The third reviewer's 18 files of several lines each, in English, German, French, Catalan, and Swedish, all read right. Of files of three lines in other code pages, Russian in Windows-1251, Greek in Windows-1253, and Japanese in Shift JIS stop, and so does "CSV (MS-DOS)"'s "Müller" in a file of one; Czech and Polish in Windows-1250, Turkish in Windows-1254 ("Ýstanbul"), and "CSV (MS-DOS)" with a line that reads clean in Mac OS Roman ("Stra·e") are rewritten wrong, the warning showing each. A one-page book whose two sidecars Excel for Mac saved, Mac OS Roman with CR LF, converts with "Café – a résumé’s red square" as its alt text and "Prices – cafés’ year by year" as its caption. The docs: `docs/sidecars.md`'s "A sidecar that isn't UTF-8", with what it can get wrong and the steps for saving one as UTF-8 by hand, in Excel, in LibreOffice (its character sets' names read from its library here), and with `iconv`; `docs/troubleshooting.md`; and the changelog's Breaking and Fixed entries.

74. **What the reviews and the mutations found.** Three separate agents reviewed the rewrite, each trying text of its own in both code pages and both line ends: the first two whole versions as they then were, the third the last revision of `misplaced` and its checks. Fixed, each with a check: ordinary text read in the wrong code page or stopping the run ("1.54 Å", "M±SD", "Ø 25 mm", "p ≤ 0.05", "100 °C", "yen (¥)", "World Bank.¹", "25˚C", "2πR"), which is why the two readings are compared by how many characters each misplaces, the five characters both read alike count for nothing, and spacing accents, superscripts, and ¥ have rules of their own; a report's UTF-8 rows read again in the code page ("H₂O", "X̄"), kept as they are now and shown; a write that failed partway leaving the sidecar cut short, now written beside it and moved into place; `shortdoi.py --dry-run` writing; copies piling up beside a file that couldn't be written, now removed when the write fails; and a rewrite as root giving a person's file to root, its owner and mode kept now. The third found that three of the last revision's four new rules made things worse on its 248 lines of alt text in English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Catalan, Italian, and the Nordic languages: a superscript between a digit and a letter ("10³m", "6.02×10²³mol", ² being a digit to Python) and any small letter after a digit ("2ƒ(x)") turned whole English Windows-1252 files into Mac OS Roman, Mac OS Roman's reading of them seldom counting anything; ä alone took German's "o. ä." and "u. ä." for Mac OS Roman's ‰, misreading a file or stopping it, as two lists of Swedish letters stopped; and the small letter after a digit stopped Mac OS Roman files with French or Catalan ordinals ("Le 2è étage", "5è curs"), whose è is a byte Windows-1252 has no character for. Narrowed as it suggested: only à and û after a digit, Mac OS Roman's ‡ and ˚ read as Windows-1252; ä only after a number, its ‰; and of the superscripts only ¹ between a digit and a letter, its π. On its lines, each alone in three setups, that reads 590 of 656 right, where the commit before the revision read 586 and the revision 566, and its 18 whole files all right, where the revision read 6; on the earlier lines it reads none worse than the revision but "The ‰ rate" and "The ‰ symbol" with CR LF, which the commit before read wrong too. Kept: a capital between capitals before a small letter, which reads Mac OS Roman's "O’Neill" and "D’Angelo" with CR LF right and "Die TÜVs" wrong. It found too that three checks would pass with the behavior broken, now each with a check of its own: the small letter after a digit ("Table 1à", "A 45û angle"), a run of letters of any script ("ªâð", Ukrainian's "Євр" in Windows-1251 read as Windows-1252, which counts now and didn't when only Latin letters made a run), and the one with fewer misplaced winning whatever the line ends prefer (a Mac OS Roman file with CR LF). Then 97 mutations of the rewrite and of the tools' wiring, each a rule or a step taken out or loosened, run on the checks that should catch it: all caught, one, the per mille rule's guard at a line's start, once its case ("ä 52") had a check of its own. Four that an earlier set missed found two checks wanting, now there (one line misplaced in both among two not stopping the run, and the copy kept beside the sidecar failing partway), and entries that did nothing, now gone: superscripts, the soft hyphen, ´, and ` among the marks text has between letters, each meeting another rule first, and ª and º among the small letters it has before a capital, which aren't Latin letters. Left, and written down in `docs/sidecars.md`: Mac OS Roman with CR LF whose characters read as plausibly in Windows-1252, a letter's name alone, a line in the code page that happens to be UTF-8, and code pages other than the two.

78. **What two reviews of it found.** Separate agents read the commit, the second after the first's findings were fixed; each ran the sidecar checks as root and as uid 1000 and 999, and the run itself as an unprivileged user on books whose sidecars root owns. Fixed, each with a check but where said. Another user's file the user can't write either, root's 0644 file to anyone else, was said to be read-only, which it isn't, and the advice was to have its owner run the conversion, which, root's or anyone's, makes the book's outputs theirs, so that the next run by someone else fails writing them (a run as root first left `page.json` root's, and the user's run stopped at it); then "replace it with a copy of your own", by `cp` and `mv`, made a colleague's shared sidecar the user's, its mode 0644, so the colleague couldn't write it, and hid that its folder couldn't be written, which the copy needs. Now another user's file is said to be theirs, its folder too where that can't be written, and what to do is replace it with a copy made with `cp -p`, which keeps its mode, or ask its owner to save it as UTF-8 with the mark; read-only means no write bit; one with a write bit this user may not write is said to be that, one root can't write (marked immutable, say) that, and one on a disk mounted read-only that alone; and besides the patched checks, a real run as `nobody` under `setpriv`, where root runs the suite, its module copied to /tmp and probed first, so that a clone or a TMPDIR uid 65534 can't reach skips it, saying why. `shortdoi.py` wrote a file the run had just said it leaves as it is; with a `.bak` it couldn't write, it asked the service and then stopped with a traceback, the lookups lost; and refusing another user's file, as the first fix had it, broke a colleague's group-writable sidecar in a shared folder, which `main` wrote in place. Now it writes in its place, as it always had, keeping the sidecar's owner, mode, and other names, and says so of another user's; it keeps the file as it was before asking anything, under the next free name (`.bak.2` where an earlier run's `.bak` is there, which it had written over); it stops before asking anything when the sidecar can't be read, written (read-only, on a disk mounted read-only, or not to be opened to write, as on Windows one Excel has open, not tried here), or kept, and a dry run says a run would stop; and a write that fails after the lookups, a disk full or an append-only file, puts the original back where it can and prints the shortDOIs found, where it had been a traceback. A setting naming a link to nothing went on without it, where one naming nothing stops the run, as the docs say: it stops again, saying where the link leads; only the default name's is gone without. `util/round-trip-decks.py` and `bin/adopt-pages.py` said a sidecar couldn't be read and then copied it, with a traceback: they skip it (`adopt-pages.py` tried as an unprivileged user, neither checked by a suite), and `round-trip-decks.py` copies `project.yaml` as before, whose loss would otherwise be silent. What to do was chosen by the error's class, every `PermissionError` "close any program that has it open": it's chosen by the error now; on Windows a sharing or lock violation (32, 33) is a program's, but replacing a file another program has open is "access denied" (5), as Git for Windows and LLVM have found, so that gets both remedies (not tried here); EACCES and EPERM are permission. A file that can't be read for another reason than permission, a disk's error or a network share gone stale, made the run go on without it, a book without what it holds: it stops the run, as it did before. The rewrite, a new file, lost the file's extended attributes, an access control list among them on Linux, which marking every sidecar would do to every one: `_owned` copies a person's own (`user.*`), the access control list, and the SELinux label, not those that describe the old contents, as integrity measurement's do (a user attribute and an access control list giving uid 1000 read and write kept, a trusted attribute not); and the new file is flushed to the disk before it's moved into place, which a crash on XFS could otherwise leave empty (checked by counting the flushes). The changelog and docs said a pipe and a link to nothing had stopped the run with a traceback, where a pipe had kept it waiting for good and a link to nothing at a sidecar's own name was passed over without a word; stated Excel's lock on Windows as fact; and claimed `shortdoi.py` caught another user's file on Windows, where nothing tells whose a file is. And the tests had covered none of `--sidecar-checked`, `IMAGE_ALT_NAME`, a configured link to nothing, or the filters' copy of `math-keep.csv`, and the uid 1000 the checks give a person's file (since Round 20) took the group down as any other user, which uses the user's own uid now. Left as it was, a judgment call for Rob: another user's sidecar that already has the mark is read without a word, nothing about it needing a person; and the run never rewrites another user's sidecar, even one it may write, where `shortdoi.py`, asked to write one, does, in place. Then 85 mutations of the reads, the rewrite, the warnings, and the tools' wiring, each run on the checks that should catch it: all caught, on the code as delivered. Found by an earlier run of them, not the reviews: the unit check of a pipe gave up with a `TimeoutError`, which is an `OSError`, which the reader took for a file it couldn't read and opened the pipe again, waiting for good (it raises an error of its own now, and again every five seconds); a reader of a sidecar whose lines end with a CR alone, which Excel 2011 for Mac wrote and a rewrite keeps, had no check of its own; and the check of the write bits in main's `_writable`, which `_kept` had come to call, had become one `_kept` makes first, so `_writable` went, `_kept` asking `os.access` itself.

79. **Pandoc 3.13: what it broke, mended, and what reading it found for older Pandocs.** Rob (2026-10-26), having tested `sidecar-utf8.mbox`: "Tests passed (2 skipped) with Pandoc 3.12.1. However, on the newly-released Pandoc 3.13 some tests fail": the convert suite's lists in quotations through Word, the LaTeX suite's list with a formula, a table, and a rule read back from Word, and the decks suite's notes slides. 3.13 and its source were fetched and its changes read before anything was run (PANDOC-NOTES). The decks failure was the suite's own: 3.13's PowerPoint writer writes the notes slide's color map that the `pptx` target had added (25bef2d, #11960), and the target already left one alone; the check expects the target's count only before 3.13 now. The other two were one change in the Word writer and reader (#9197): an item's later paragraphs are unnumbered and indented like the item's text, where 3.12.1 numbered each in a blank-marker list, and the reader keeps a paragraph so indented in the item and ends every list it has open at anything else. A formula in an item, which the target still numbered as the older writer did, ended the item; so did a table, a rule, or a figure in it, the figure paired with its caption now that its picture isn't numbered, its caption's words a quotation inside the caption; and so did a quotation or code in an item, which the target indents beyond the item's text so its depth survives. What followed came back as quotations, and the list's later items as a list of their own. **The change**: `docxtarget` follows the writer it runs (`pandoc_version`, `CONTINUATION_PANDOC`), a formula in an item given the item's indent from 3.13, and its file says so in a document variable (`TextbookImproverContinuations`); reading such a file, `docxrepair.item_paragraphs` mirrors 3.13's reader (its open lists, and which of them the reader has ended at something the item holds), and `mark_continuations` lines a quote's or code's paragraph up with the item's text, marked with its depth, numbers as a list paragraph (an id with no definition, and no indent) each paragraph the reader would keep in no list, and takes the indent off a held figure's paragraphs and a held table's caption; `apply_list_tables` puts a figure back in its item as it does a table or a rule; with a reader before 3.13, every such paragraph is a list paragraph, as an older file's are. A paragraph in the writer's form that no open list lines up with (what follows a heading in an item; the words of an item the writer numbered nowhere, in a file written before) is a list paragraph at its level, as 3.12.1 had it, not a quotation. The first review (item 80) found more the reader ends a list at, each mirrored now: a note, whose paragraphs it reads at the reference (`notePartsToBlocks` keeps no list open across them), after which the item's paragraphs before the note are list paragraphs too, since the reader folds one only into the item's own paragraph just before it (`handleListParagraphs`); a caption after a table, which it pairs with the table (`addCaptioned`, mirrored as `docxtarget.captioned_parts`, which also counts the reader's figures for the target's marks); and a table's cells, read from cell to cell. A figure of two pictures, which the writer writes as a table, is held as one. And the target counts the blocks the reader gives back after something an item holds as the reader groups list items (`flatToBullets'`), a list the item holds split where its items hold a table too, and the reading puts an outer item's blocks back first (item 80). **With either Pandoc**: a table's caption in a list item, which the writer gives the item's Compact style (a `Plain` caption takes the list's style over Table Caption), read back as a paragraph beside the caption the reader took from `w:tblCaption`, the caption twice and the list ended there (Table 11.21, item 11-5's list split in two): the target styles it Table Caption now (`table_captions`), and reading a file written before makes the paragraph the table's caption; a quotation's mark, `tiqItemQuote1x1`, was left on a page as an empty anchor where it was the page's only change (`nest_item_quotes` didn't count it); an item that opens with anchors before a list, as the solution to Example 2.17 has its parts, or with a table, a figure of two pictures, or a rule, got no number from either writer, lost in Word and in reading (`_number_anchored`: the anchors a paragraph of their own, an empty paragraph before the table or rule, as the writer puts one before a list); a formula alone in a `Plain`, in a tight item, ended the list; and a list in an item came apart where both items held a table or a rule, or the outer item had a paragraph after the inner list (the count above). **Found reading 3.13's changes, fixed for older Pandocs**: a table of 10 columns or more with a line break or a block in a cell was the text `[TABLE]` in a `markdown` target (#11945; written as HTML now, as a table with merged cells is); and a PDF stopped on a definition list's term with an `=` in it, which LaTeX's tagging took for keys in `\item[...]` (#11954; braced now, as 3.13 does). Documented, not changed: 3.13 reads YAML 1.2, so `toc: no` gives a contents page and a key given twice stops the build (measured). **Measured** on *Introductory Business Statistics 2e*'s HTML, 169 pages, through the Word target and back, compared with `util/compare-output.py` against the book converted directly: with the old code, 68 pages came back the same with either Pandoc; 3.12.1 left 21 pages' lists unlike the source's (10 with a list too many or too few) and 10 pages' figures pictures, and 3.13 25 pages' lists (16), quotations on 10 pages, and figures out of their lists. With the new code, 72 pages come back the same, written and read with 3.13, with 3.12.1, or written with 3.13 and read with 3.12.1; no page has a quotation; and the lists of only 5 pages differ with 3.13, 6 with 3.12.1 reading. The 5 are key-terms pages, whose definitions hold lists, which come back after their definitions, splitting the definition list (3 lists come back as 5, say), with either Pandoc, the old code too; the sixth, *2-2*, has a paragraph between two lists in an item, which reading before 3.13 puts in the first list's last item, the second list then joining it, one list fewer. From a file written with 3.13, whichever reads it, every figure is back in its item but the 7 that open theirs (2.36, 3.22, 8.18 to 8.22), which come back as their pictures and captions; from one written with 3.12.1, figures on 10 pages come back as pictures, as before. The rest of each run's differences, the same before and after, are pictures under Word's names (73 pages), word counts (36), formulas (7), and one page's tables, as a book read back from Word has them. What's left, each a limit the docs state: an item's paragraph after a list in it that comes back a list paragraph goes into that list's last item (with a Pandoc reading before 3.13, and with 3.13 where the item holds a table, a rule, or a figure before that list, or a note in the inner list's item; TI's 3.12.1 path did this before); a caption of more than one paragraph keeps one in the caption; a figure or table in a div with more in it, a credit say, still ends the list with 3.13; a list in a note comes back as paragraphs, and a list in a definition after the definition, as Pandoc's reader reads them (both versions; PANDOC-NOTES); a definition list in an item comes back as its term and a paragraph; a figure that opens its item comes back its picture and caption, the writer numbering the picture's paragraph; a figure of two pictures in an item written before 3.13 still ends the list; and an item that opens with a quotation, or holds a table in a quotation, comes back wrong with either Pandoc, as before. Not tried in Word or with a screen reader.

80. **What two reviews and the mutations of it found.** A separate agent read the round's diff with both Pandocs and their source and round-tripped its own pages through the Word target under 3.13, 3.12.1, and each written with one and read with the other; a second read the code as fixed, the same way. an outer item's paragraph holding a note after its list went into the list's last item, with 3.13, where the old code had it right, the note making list paragraphs of the item's paragraphs before it, which the reader folds into the item just before, the nested one (not once a deeper item has opened now); a tight definition list after a table or a rule an item held, which the reader gives back as more blocks than the item held, the definition in the item's style, left its last block out of the item, and the list split, with 3.13 as with 3.12.1 (what's left before the list begins again goes back in the item whose list goes on); sibling items that each open with an anchor before a list, as *Introductory Business Statistics 2e*'s solution to Example 2.17 has them, fused into one list of six, the writer numbering neither item (an item that opens with anchors before a list gets a paragraph of them for its number now, with either Pandoc); a note that ends with a list left that list's level open to the reader, which took the item's next paragraph, a list paragraph keeping its indent, for the note's list's, as it did with the old code (a list paragraph has no indent now, which only Pandoc reads); And some the old code had too: a formula alone in a `Plain`, in a tight item, ended the list with either Pandoc (`_display_math_para` and `_split_display` take a `Plain` now, and a span holding only a formula, as the writer's `isDisplayMath` does); an outer item's paragraph after an inner item's held table, and held blocks at two levels, came back outside the list or in the wrong item, which the counting below mends; and a caption of two paragraphs and a figure in a div with a credit, limits the docs state now. Case #2 was item 78's second judgment call: the run never rewrites another user's sidecar, even one it may write, since the new file would be the runner's. **The change** (5176302): another user's sidecar that nothing but whose it is keeps the run from rewriting, as nothing would were it the runner's, is a warning now whatever it holds, one of ASCII alone too, which had been a note, and the warning says it *isn't* given the mark, or *isn't* rewritten as UTF-8, rather than that it can't be (`sidecars._theirs`, whose reason carries a third item saying so, and `_because`). One the run couldn't rewrite were it the user's (read-only, another name linked to it, or in a folder that can't be written) is said to be that and theirs, in a note when it holds nothing outside ASCII, as one's own is. A link says whose file it leads to, and a copy can take a link's place where the link is the user's, whatever folder its file is in. The docs give `mv -f`, without which `mv` asks before it replaces a file the user may not write, and how `ls -ld` shows the sticky bit, a `t` or a `T`. A run as root that couldn't give a rewritten sidecar its owner, as root in a user namespace (a rootless container) can't give a file a user outside it has, had made the sidecar the runner's, saying only that the mark was added: the new file's owner is checked before it's moved into place now, and a sidecar whose owner couldn't be kept is left as it is and said to be another user's (`OwnerLost`), its owner named as the namespace sees it (`nobody`). Root there that may not write a file of a user outside the namespace, which it sees as the kernel's overflow uid, nobody, said in a note that the file couldn't be written "though it has a write bit (marked immutable, say)" and to make it writable: it's another user's now, warned of (`_overflow_uid`), found mutating the code below. Root's own file that root can't write is still said to be marked immutable, say, and so is another user's outside a namespace, as a network share mapping root to nobody would have it (not tried). 83. **Words beside a long fill-in blank keep their line where they fit it.** Rob (2026-10-27): "Also go ahead and fix the issue with counting widths for the fill-in blanks." What was left, found before fixing: a table without widths fits its line by each column's widest paragraph set as one line, and the measure counted a blank whole in that, so a long blank took the line from the words beside it, which wrapped where they had room, though in LuaLaTeX the blank is drawn as long as its column leaves room for. **The change** (9497295): where the cells fit the line with each blank at its least, each column is as wide as it needs to be so and the columns of blanks share the rest by how much longer their blanks are whole (`steps_next` in `latexbuild.FIT_MACROS`, a worked example's steps' reasons too, which the same measure lays out). A blank's least is three underscores, or, where words share its line, before it or joined to it as far as a space TeX may break at, a no-break space not one, two thirds of the line: the blank macros draw a long blank at two thirds of its line while TeX breaks a paragraph and ask TeX to end the line after it, so a column less than three times as wide as the blank's label puts the blank on the line after the label. The first version, which took a blank's least as three underscores whatever its label, did that: "Signature:" alone on its line beside words on one, the blank below it. A paragraph's measure is a function of its own now, `oerfit.paragraph`, which the PDF suite runs by `texlua`. Where the words don't fit the line beside the blanks at their least, the line is shared as before, the blank counted whole, and so it is by the widths `pdf-target.lua` counts for a table's first run, which a table with a cell across columns keeps, LaTeX measuring none, and a TeX without Lua sets, where a blank is drawn whole (item 84). **Measured** on the 182 tables without widths that hold a blank in the 14 CNX books with any, their tables in a book of their own (`r24/bc`), built with `main`'s code and with this, and with the first version, which laid every one of them out as this does: 2 are laid out differently, each with its words on fewer lines and its blanks shorter, on the lines they were on (*Algebra 1*'s 5.6.2, "Volume of Coral (cubic centimeters)" on one line, not two; *College Algebra with Corequisite Support 2e*'s 7.7, two steps' words each on one line, not two); the rest as they were, but for where one breaks across pages. **Checks** (the PDF suite's fit book): a table of seven words beside "Signature:" and a blank of 66 underscores, its words on one line where they had been on two, and one of a name and a role beside a blank of 58, each on one where each had been on two, each blank drawn shorter to end at its column's edge; a third whose words fit beside "Labelsig:" and a blank of three underscores but not beside one of two thirds of a column three times the label's width, the blank on the label's line and the words wrapping; and `oerfit.paragraph`'s least of eight paragraphs, on nodes a character wide: a label's blank, text and a formula joined to one, a no-break space after one, several blanks, and none. 87. **Every PDF draws LaTeX's picture mode with pict2e, and `picture_paths: off` keeps LaTeX's own.** Rob (2026-10-27), shown a figure drawn both ways (Round 25's `r25/pict`), asked whether a circle meant to be 40 points would come out at 80; told the other way round, that LaTeX draws a circle asked for at 80 points at 40, its font's largest, and pict2e draws it at 80, as written, so the risk is a picture laid out around what LaTeX drew: "OK, then using pict2e by default sounds like the best choice. If we can add an option to turn that behavior off, that would be good insurance for the failure mode we're worried about." **The change**: `latexbuild.PICTURE_PATHS`, item 48's `CANCEL_STROKES` renamed, loads pict2e for every PDF, a book's, a deck's, and a LaTeX book's tagged copy, where it had loaded it for cancel alone, at `\begin{document}` and with its own drawing commands set aside and given back as before, `\buttcap` among them, which pict2e's `\circle`, `\dot`, and `\oval` call, and which are given pict2e's own in the group each draws in: taken away, as it was while pict2e drew only cancel's lines, it stopped LaTeX at the first circle ("Undefined control sequence"), as the LaTeX suite's new checks found, and kept for them, a document's own was replaced (item 92); `\maxovalrad`, which `\oval` reads, is set aside too, given back where the document had one, and kept where it hadn't; and the trig package's names, which pict2e loads and uses, `\UseSin` and the rest, stay trig's, a document's own replaced, as where cancel loaded pict2e before. `picture_paths` (`on`, the default, or `off`; a render setting, so a target's intermediates are shared) writes `\OERPictureFonts` before it where it's off (`PICTURE_FONTS`), and pict2e is then loaded only where cancel is, for the struck-out term's strokes, as before, and draws any picture in the document too: off is LaTeX's own picture mode only in a document that loads no cancel, which Pandoc's template loads for a formula that strikes a term out, and a LaTeX book may itself (the setting's description had said only the first). `texremediate.tag` adds `PICTURE_PATHS` to a LaTeX book's tagged copy with the setting on, and with it off only where the book loads cancel, after `PICTURE_FONTS`; the run's line for the copy says "its drawings in picture mode drawn with paths by pict2e, not a font's glyphs (picture_paths)" where it has a `picture` environment. A TeX without pict2e now stops every PDF, not only one that strikes a term out, the run's advice naming pict2e and cancel together (`failure_advice`); pict2e is in TeX Live's `collection-pictures`, and TinyTeX installs it with `tlmgr install pict2e`, which the installation page's first `tlmgr` line has. A fallback to LaTeX's own picture mode with a warning, as the faces fall back to Latin Modern (item 85), would keep a book with no picture building without it; not built. **Checks**: the LaTeX suite's struck-out case: a document with no cancel loads pict2e, its circle asked for at 80 points a path, no glyph of `lcircle10`; with `PICTURE_FONTS` it loads none, LaTeX drawing the circle with `lcircle10`'s glyphs; with `PICTURE_FONTS` and cancel, pict2e is loaded for the struck-out term and draws the picture too, one diagonal stroke and no `lcircle10`; a document's own `\buttcap` and `\maxovalrad` kept, its circles, oval, and dot drawn by pict2e all the same, four curves each; and what a tagged copy gets, the macros and the count, with the setting on, off, and off with cancel, and a book's copies as the run makes them with a target's setting each way, the run saying so of the first. The decks suite: a deck's circle, its target's `picture_paths` off, in `LCIRCLE10`'s glyphs. The PDF suite: the untagged book, its target's `picture_paths` off, draws its page's 80-point circle with `LCIRCLE10`, and the preamble book, in the default, with neither `LINE10` nor `LCIRCLE10`, and its circle four curves, where the check had looked only for the fonts' absence, which a picture dropped would pass (item 92). Docs: `formats.md`'s PDF section, `latex.md`, `installation.md`, `testing.md`, the setting's description (`conversion-settings.md`), and the CHANGELOG's Breaking entry. A PDF (`pdf-target.lua`'s `ROW_RULES` and `rule_rows`, `PDF_MACROS`' `\OERRowRules`): none of the writer's `\toprule`, `\midrule`, and `\bottomrule`, each defined to nothing in the table's group (the `\noalign{}` after each left alone), and booktabs' `\specialrule` under each row, a `\midrule`'s width (`\lightrulewidth`, 0.6 points in 12-point type) and space above and below (`\aboverulesep`, `\belowrulesep`), in OpenStax's gray (`\CT@arc@`, booktabs' hook for colortbl's color).
