89. **A formula in running text that its page sets in display style is so where `math.display_style_in_text` says, off by default.** Rob (2026-10-27), of Round 19's open question: "I think our default should be not to use display style in running text, but we could add a configuration option to honor it. I assume this is a more general question than simply for the CNX reader, at least in theory." It is: Pandoc's HTML reader drops MathML's display style, an `mstyle` with `displaystyle="true"` or a `math` element's own (PANDOC-NOTES), on any HTML page, so the setting is the run's, not the unpacker's. **The change**: `lib/mathstyle.py` holds what the unpacker's steps had (item 63's `_style_set` and `_displayed`, now `style_set` and `displayed`, which `cnx.steptables` calls), and `marked_in_text`, which `convert.py` runs on every HTML page before Pandoc reads it, after its repairs: a formula in running text or a table's cell, not `display="block"` and not marked already (a step's `displaystyle` span, or one of its own from an earlier run), that sets in display style something display style draws otherwise (a fraction, a large operator, an operator's limits under and over it) goes in a span of class `displaystyle-text`, the markup edited as text a formula at a time, each found as an HTML parser finds it (`_Formulas`), not one in a comment, a script, or an attribute's value, the rest as it was; and so does a target's variant of a page (`read_variants`). Marking at reading, whatever the setting, keeps one reading for every target, since the reading stage's environment has no target's settings; `math-repair.lua`, a filter-stage filter, then sets each marked formula in display style after its repairs, so that its TeX is the same to `math-repaired.csv` and `math-keep.csv` whatever the setting, `\displaystyle` opening it, where the target's `math.display_style_in_text` (`MATH_DISPLAY_STYLE_IN_TEXT`, a filter setting, so targets that differ get intermediates of their own) is true, as `html-source.lua` sets a formula of the class `displaystyle`, which a page's and an EPUB's MathML then carry as an `mstyle` (`target-blocks.lua`) and a Word file doesn't, and either way takes the span away where it holds nothing else. The run says how many it kept, on how many pages, counted in the pages each target that sets it reads, its variants among them, and by which targets where not every one. OpenStax's CNXML sets 6,768 formulas in running text and 473 in a table's cell in display style where it changes them, 6,066 of the first in the calculus books, in English and in Spanish (`r26/scripts/display_census.py`, by `mathstyle.in_display`); Round 19's census (`r18/scripts/inlinedisp.py`), which counted a formula in an equation as in running text, had found 4,723 with that round's code, as the open question below has it; counted its way with today's, it's 9,207 (`display_census2.py`). **Measured** on *Calculus Volume 2*'s third chapter (`r26/books/cv3`, `measure26.sh`), a target with the setting beside one without: 551 formulas kept in display style, on 10 of its 12 pages, as the run says, and its PDF 132 pages, where it's 121 without (the two built in 902 seconds, the pages read once). **Checks**: the convert suite's display-style page, with a paragraph holding a formula so set: kept in display style, its TeX opening with `\displaystyle`, by a target with the setting, and in text style, no span left, by one without; and the unit suite's (`check_display_style_in_text`): a fraction, a sum's limits, and a formula whose `math` element says so marked; a letter, an accent, a fraction in a script, one display style is turned off for again inside, a display formula, and one marked already not; and the rest of the page as it was. Docs: `html.md`, `cnx-input.md`, the setting's description, and the CHANGELOG.

90. **A step's display style is the whole formula's, written down.** Rob (2026-10-27), of Round 19's open question, display style kept to the part of a step's formula OpenStax set so: "Let's just document this and leave it alone." `cnx-input.md` says so where it describes a step's display style: once Pandoc has read a formula, the part can't be told from the rest, so the whole formula is in display style, an integrand beside an integral sign OpenStax set so alone a little larger than OpenStax sets it, and keeping display style to the part would take the unpacker writing the formula's TeX itself, which it doesn't. Nothing else changed.

91. **Code is set at the text's size, and a block of code too wide for its line is fitted to it.** Rob (2026-10-27), of the open question item 85 left, code in Plex Mono at 0.858 of the text's size or at the text's with a line of code fitted to its line, having pushed `plex-default.mbox`: "I think it's worth also setting the code at the text's size and fitting lines the way tables are." **The change**: `build-pdf.py`'s `PLEX_MONO_SCALE` is gone, and Plex Mono is scaled as Pandoc's template scales every face but the text's, to the text face's small letters (`Scale=MatchLowercase`), which beside Plex Serif, whose small letters are as tall (516 units of 1,000 in each), is the text's size: 65 characters fill the default page's line at 12 points. `pdf-target.lua` numbers each block of code not in a table and sets it between `\OERFitCode` and `\OERFitCodeEnd`, a group, a footnote's `\OERCodeFile` (`footnote-code.lua`) too; `FIT_MACROS` measures each of its lines as LaTeX sets it, fancyvrb's (highlighted code, and code in a footnote) by the box its characters are set in, through `\FancyVerbFormatLine`, which the group wraps and unpacks as it was, and LaTeX's verbatim's (code in no language), a paragraph a line, by its line less the glue at its edges (`oer.fit.cells`), not what the output routine sets while the group is open across a page's break; and it fits the block as it fits a formula in text (kind `c`): its type set smaller, as much as its longest line takes, to three quarters of its size at least, not centered, so that a line still too long runs on into the margin on its right, and smaller still, to half at least, where it would come within a quarter inch of the paper's edge there, the right margin's width whatever the left's, fitted again on the second run where it's still too wide (Latin Modern Mono's 8-point design, used from 8.5 points down, is 3 percent wider for its size than its 12-point one), and nothing narrowed, since its spaces are characters. A footnote's code is fitted to the footnote's line, a footnote's in a table's cell too, and a quotation's to the quotation's; code in a table's cell isn't fitted itself, its table is, a line of code measured as a piece TeX can't break. LaTeX's verbatim no longer breaks a line after a hyphen, as ragged right let it. The build's fit report counts blocks of code with the tables and formulas, names a block still wider than the text, by how far it runs past the text's edge, running into the margin (`fit_report`), and warns of one too wide for the paper; `overfull_lines` leaves a block's lines to it, LaTeX reporting a line of its verbatim as a line of text too wide and fancyvrb's not at all, and knows them by the lines each block prints in LaTeX's output as it begins and ends (`CODE_MARKS`), since LaTeX names a footnote's line of code by the line of the file it's read from. The latex target's LaTeX keeps the marks, and `latexsource.fit_marks` takes them out when it's read back, a line at a time, since LaTeX's verbatim holds braces that don't pair. A deck's PDF fits a slide's code the same way. **Measured**: OpenStax's books have 667 blocks of code as the unpacker takes them (`r26/scripts/code_census2.py`, its newline elements line breaks and the indentation its lines share taken off, as the review counted them from the unpacked books; the first census had counted lines a newline element joined as one, item 92), 119 with a line longer than 65 characters (74 in *Principles of Data Science*, 41 in *Introduction to Python Programming*), 46 longer than 86, which run into the margin at three quarters of their size, 32 longer than 97, set smaller still, and 7 longer than 145, too long for the paper even at half, 5 of them in *Principles of Data Science* (up to 749 characters, a paragraph written as a string) and 2 in *Introduction to Python Programming*: wrapping a line would keep those on the paper, which nothing does. **Checks**: the PDF suite's code book, in Plex and in Latin Modern: a block whose lines fit at the text's size; a highlighted line too long and one in no language set smaller to fit, the block's other lines with them; a line in a list's item that fits the text's width fitted to the item's line; a line in no language too long even at three quarters set at three quarters, running into the margin, named as code and not as a line of text too wide; one that would come within a quarter inch of the paper's edge set smaller to end that far inside it, in Latin Modern Mono too, whose smallest design is wider for its size; one too long for the paper even at half set at half and warned of; a footnote's fitted to the footnote's line; each line's text as written; and veraPDF finding nothing; and the cases of item 92: a line with hyphens fitted whole, a quotation's line, a definition that opens with code, code in a table's cell, in no language in one table and highlighted in another, a footnote's in one, a footnote's line still too wide and a footnote's words too wide, a one-sided page with a wider right margin, a numbered display on it too, a list's line in an untagged PDF too, where LaTeX's own verbatim indents it by its left skip, and a list's code under a footer across pages. And the two-column book's line of code too wide for its column even at three quarters of its size, in Latin Modern Mono, fitted again on the second run; the default book's code at the text's size, the unit suite's reports (`check_code_fit_report`), the decks suite's slide of code too wide, fitted, smaller than a slide's code that fits, and a section's footnote's code at its size, and the LaTeX suite's latex target marking each block, a footnote's too, and reading back to the same pages. Docs: `formats.md`'s PDF section and its latex target's, `configuration.md`'s "The faces", `slides.md`, `latex.md`, `testing.md`, and the CHANGELOG, the Plex entry's sentence on code's size changed.

92. **What the reviews of Round 26 found.** Two separate agents read the change: the first the pict2e, rules, and display-style commits, against Pandoc 3.13's writer, longtable 4.27, booktabs, latex-lab's firstaid and block modules, pict2e and trig, and ce-styles' corn design, building small books with each edge case of the row rules it could think of (a table of the class `float`, an empty last cell, a cell across columns, a foot, a caption, a table in a cell, tables of exactly 200 rows with and without a head, page breaks), each ruled right, tagged and untagged, and veraPDF finding nothing; the second the code commit. **Fixed**, each with a check: `marked_in_text` found a formula by a pattern that didn't know a comment, a script, or an attribute's value, so the words `<math>` in a comment or an `alt` ran its span from inside them to the next formula's end, taking a French span's last words out of it, and losing an image's alt text and a formula, on any page, the setting on or off, since the marking runs on every page: each formula is found as an HTML parser finds it now (`_Formulas`); a formula in display style that math repair changed got `\displaystyle` before it was repaired, so a `math-keep.csv` row copied from a target without the setting kept nothing in one with it: the setting is applied after the repairs; a target's variant of an HTML page wasn't marked: it is, and the run counts what each target reads; pict2e for every PDF replaced a document's own `\buttcap`, which the first version kept from the names set aside since pict2e's `\circle` and `\oval` call it, and a document's own `\maxovalrad` stopped pict2e loading: `\buttcap` is set aside with the rest, pict2e's three commands given its own, and `\maxovalrad` set aside and given back; the preamble book's check of its circle looked only for the fonts' absence, which a picture dropped passes: it counts the circle's four curves (`pdftext.curves`); OpenStax rules a calculus book's Key Equations in Grey1, #F1F1F1, and only a table classed `unstyled`, not in Grey3 whatever its class (`row-rules-faint`); it draws no rule under an unstyled table's head, which the first version drew in every format; the count of tables with a cell spanning rows had left out the design's four Spanish books (6 of 3,337, not of 3,133); and `picture_paths`' description said a struck-out term where for a LaTeX book it's loading cancel. Found while fixing those: a ruled table in the latex target's LaTeX, read back as a source, gained an empty paragraph, the reader expanding `\OERRowRules` as the preamble defines it; `latexsource.repair_text` drops both commands now. **Left**: a `\maxovalrad` made in a document's text, and a command of one of the trig package's names, which pict2e loads, stop LaTeX or are replaced by trig's, as where cancel loaded pict2e before (documented). And outside the change: `lib/mathjax.py` takes a MathJax rendering followed by a `<script type="math/mml">` for one whose TeX follows it and drops the rendering, but Pandoc reads only `math/tex` scripts, so the formula is lost (`mathjax.rebuilt` on such a page keeps the script alone, which `html-raw.lua` drops); not fixed then, fixed in item 98. The second agent, of the code commit, built a small book or deck for each case it thought of, a page's footer, a deck's section, a definition, a quotation, a table's cell, and found thirteen things. **Fixed**, each with a check: a definition that opens with code lost its term's line, the writer's `~` before such a block (`\item[term] ~`, its #4662) gone with the mark first, and LaTeX set the term in the code's first line, or the next list's: the definition opens with a no-break space again, which reads back as the writer's own does; reading the `latex` target back stopped on a footnote that opens with code ("unexpected ()"), whose mark the writer sets after `\footnote{`, where the pattern took only a mark on a line of its own (`latexsource.FIT_CODE_MARK`); a page's footer, which the output routine sets while a block's group is open across a page's break, was measured as the block's lines, and a list's code set at 90 percent under a long footer: nothing the output routine sets is measured (`status.output_active`), a wrapping table's cells across a page's break having had the same flaw; a deck's section's footnotes, which deck-pdf.lua runs pdf-target.lua on apart from the deck, numbered their fits from 1, as the deck does, so a section's code took the deck's first fit and was set at 69 percent though it fit: each section's are numbered from a number of their own (`OER_FIT_FIRST`); latex-lab's verbatim, whose right skip is the paragraph's, which ragged right stretches, broke a line of code too long after a hyphen, and the measure took each piece for a line: verbatim doesn't break after one now (`\exhyphenpenalty`), as LaTeX's own, whose right skip doesn't stretch, never did; a footnote's line of code in no language still too wide was named twice, as code and as a line of text, LaTeX naming it by the line of the file it's read from, and a footnote's own words too wide, whose last block is code, not at all, LaTeX naming them by the line the footnote's text ends on, in the block's lines: the build knows code's lines by what each block prints in LaTeX's output as it begins and ends (`CODE_MARKS`); a footnote's code in a table's cell, which the writer sets after the table, wasn't fitted, and is; code in a table's cell, whose table the docs said was fitted for it, wasn't, the cell measured by the pieces between its spaces, and a line of highlighted code not at all: a line of code is a piece TeX can't break, as words a no-break space joins now are, and a highlighted line is measured through `\FancyVerbFormatLine` for the innermost fit; how far code, a formula in text, or a numbered display may run into the margin was set by the narrower of the page's margins, a left one narrower than the right among them: it's the right one's (`\__oer_fit_right_margin:`), the narrower of two on a two-sided page; a quotation's code, fitted to the quotation's line and inside the text's, was said to run into the margin: a block is named by how far it runs past the text's edge; the decks suite's code passed fitted or not, its line fitting the slide at the text's size: it's longer, and checked against a slide's code that fits; 100. **A block of code too long for the paper even at half its size wraps.** Rob (2026-10-28), of the 7 blocks item 91 left, which only wrapping would keep on the paper: "Go ahead and build wrapping for the too-wide code." Built for those, as I read it: a block whose longest line would come within a quarter inch of the paper's edge even at half its size, which ran off the paper with a warning, is set at three quarters of its size, the least every other fit keeps to where it can, and each of its lines too long for its line is wrapped where it reaches the line's end, the text's edge or a quotation's or a list's item's, not into the margin; every other block is fitted as before, a line that fits at three quarters running into the margin, and one that doesn't set smaller, to half at least. Wrapping at the text's size, or in place of the sizes below three quarters, is offered to Rob (Open questions).

**How.** `oerfit.next` gives a block of code (kind `c`) a state that wraps, at `FIT_FLOOR`, where its width at `FIT_LEAST` is still wider than its room on the paper. The state goes in the `.aux` as `\OERFitState`, and after it `\ifdefined\OERFitWrap\OERFitWrap{id}\fi`, so macros from before read past it (shown: `main`'s macros read a new `.aux` without an error), and `\OERFitApply` has a seventh argument for it. A wrapped block (`\__oer_fit_wrap:`) marks what it holds (`\OERFitWrapAttribute`), and sets its lines touching where they'd come closer than its spacing, with nothing between them (`\lineskip`, `\lineskiplimit`). Its lines are paragraphs, which TeX breaks: LaTeX's verbatim's (code in no language) are paragraphs already, and a line of fancyvrb's (highlighted code, and a footnote's) too long for its line is set as one, in a box where fancyvrb puts the line's (`\__oer_fit_wrap_line:`), as fvextra sets a line it breaks (fvextra 1.14.0's `\parbox[t]`), untagged as a paragraph, its text the line's (`block/verbatim/codeline`). The box is as wide as the line the fit measured the block against, the `\linewidth` at `\OERFitCode`, from where fancyvrb's line begins: fancyvrb's own line is the text's width less the left margins, a quotation's right margin in it. Such a box is as deep as its lines, from the first one's base, and TeX set the next line under it by that depth with `\lineskip` between, so the line after a wrapped one came closer than the block's spacing, over the wrapped one's last part (seen in the prototype): each of fancyvrb's lines in such a block holds a strut, the line's height above its base and its depth below, so that, touching, each is at the block's spacing, as fvextra does. `oer.fit.wrap`, a `pre_linebreak_filter`, takes a paragraph whose first glyph is marked, not one the output routine sets: it measures the paragraph whole, before it's broken, for the fit, where verbatim's lines had been measured as broken, by what it holds, summed in Lua, as fancyvrb's line is measured by what its box holds, since TeX can't read a width past `\maxdimen`; leaves it unbroken where it's within half a point (`TOLERANCE`) of its line, as fancyvrb's line is (the second review's word); flattens its discretionaries; lets TeX break after a run of spaces, no-break spaces among them, a penalty of 0 after its last space, so the space stays at the line's end, where tagpdf writes it as a space character, and a broken line's text is the line's: the penalty has the attributes of the character before the space, since a line's right skip takes those of the break it ends at (shown on a paragraph of its own), and with the space's, tagpdf wrote a second space at each break, while a break before the space lost it; and between two characters, with a penalty of 120 after a mark and of 150 between two letters or digits, so a word longer than the line breaks after a comma, a bracket, or a dot where it can; 120 squared, 14,400 demerits, is more than a part a space ends can cost with the right skip below, (10 + 100)², 12,100, at most, so a word that fits the next row whole goes there (a penalty of 50 broke it after a dot). A character of no width, as a combining mark is once it's set, isn't parted from the letter it's on: the letter before it, but for a mark of a right-to-left script (U+0590 to U+08FF, and the Hebrew and Arabic presentation forms) in a font HarfBuzz shapes, luaotfload's harf mode, as the fallback fonts are loaded (`fonts.hashes.identifiers[font].hb`), which sets the mark before its letter, where node mode sets it after (both shown on a Hebrew word in DejaVu Sans): no break before a mark that belongs to what's before it, nor after one that belongs to what's after it. A run of blanks is one place to break, after its last, the line's indentation too, never inside it; TeX takes the break after the indentation only where the parts after it have more room than the indentation leaves its row, which with the hang below is only a line indented deeper than leaves 20 characters (`ROOM`), whose text then starts on the next row where its first word doesn't fit beside it; elsewhere a long word after the indentation breaks where the row ends. Each part after the first hangs the line's indentation and two characters further in, its leading spaces counted and no-break spaces among them, as OpenStax indents code with them, a character as wide as the line's first that has a width, but no further than leaves it 20 characters: the left skip is that much wider and a kern takes it back from the first line, which a list's paragraph shape doesn't override, as it does `\hangindent`. The right skip ends a part at the line's end, the line the fit measured the block against (`oerfit.right`, from `\OERFitCode`), whatever the paragraph's own: LaTeX's verbatim sets only a left skip, and latex-lab's a paragraph shape (as of LaTeX 2026-06-01), which in a quotation is 30 points shorter than the quotation's line. It stretches as far as the line is wide, so TeX fills a line before it breaks one; nothing is hyphenated; and the interline penalty is 10,000, so a line's parts stay on a page together, as a box's do, unless they take more than half the page (`\vsize`): `oer.fit.unwrap` then takes the 10,000 back off the penalties between them, and a line in no language breaks across pages, as a paragraph's lines do; a highlighted line's box can't. `oer.fit.unwrap`, after the break, puts the paragraph's settings back, and notes whether a line of fancyvrb's is taller than the page. The run's report says which blocks it wrapped (`TextbookImprover fit wrapped:` in LaTeX's log, which `fit_report` reads), where it had warned of them as too wide for the paper, and warns of a highlighted line too long for a page even wrapped, which runs off its page's foot (`TextbookImprover fit tall:`).

**Measured.** The PDF suite's code book, on the default page in Plex Mono and in Latin Modern Mono: a line of one word 200 characters long, broken between its letters; a line of a word TeX would hyphenate, not hyphenated; a line of words indented with spaces and one indented with no-break spaces, broken at their spaces; lines in no language, LaTeX's verbatim's, one of hyphened words broken after a hyphen; a long word after an indentation of 60 spaces, broken in the word; a line indented 90 spaces, deeper than leaves 20 characters, its text 20 characters from the line's end; a line of words joined by no-break spaces, broken after one; a word after a space that fits the next row whole, moved there; a line that opens with a mark, its parts two characters in; a line in no language longer than its line by less than half a point, not broken; Hebrew with its points, and a line with a point on every letter, each part holding each letter's points, where a font has Hebrew, as DejaVu Sans, a fallback, does here; and a line at a page's foot, whose parts go on to the next page together: each at three quarters, every part inside the text's width, each part after the first its line's indentation and two characters in, the line after each at the block's spacing, and each line's text in the PDF's structure as written, its spaces kept. On a page with a wider right margin, a quotation's lines, highlighted and in no language, in a tagged PDF and an untagged one, end at the quotation's line. On a page 4 inches tall, a highlighted line of 5,000 characters, wider at 12 points than TeX's largest dimension and than a box's width TeX can hold, wraps and is said to run off its page; and a line in no language as long breaks across six pages, nothing off the paper. On OpenStax's books, the six pages that hold the 7 blocks, unpacked and built alone (*Principles of Data Science*'s 2.3, 4.2, 9.1, and 10.3, and *Introduction to Python Programming*'s 2.7 and 14.3), built again with the change as the review left it: the 7 wrapped at three quarters, where `main` set them at half and warned that they ran off the paper; every other line of code the same size as on `main` (264 rows of the one and 39 of the other compared, all but the wrapped blocks' the same); nothing of *Principles of Data Science*'s within a quarter inch of the paper's edge, and of *Introduction to Python Programming*'s only the inline code in 14.3 (below), which runs off the paper on `main` too; veraPDF 1.30.3 passes both. A deck's code too wide for its slide even at half wraps the same, veraPDF passing. 103. **A list's item that opens with highlighted code keeps its number under tagging.** Rob (2026-10-28), of the lost number Round 28's review found (item 101): "yes, let's try to diagnose and fix that." LaTeX's tagging code for lists (`latex-lab-testphase-block.sty`, LaTeX 2026-06-01) keeps an item's label in `\g__block_labels_box`, not in `\@labels`, and sets it when the item's first paragraph begins, from the `para/begin` hook (`\__block_item_everypar_std:`). fancyvrb, which Pandoc sets highlighted code in (`Highlighting`), begins no paragraph: its list sets `\@inlabel` false (`\FV@ListVSpace`) and puts `\@labels` beside its first line (`\FV@ListProcessLine@i`), which the tagging code leaves empty; latex-lab's first aid for fancyvrb (`latex-lab-testphase-firstaid.sty`) keeps that and doesn't reach the tagging code's box. So the label waited for the next item's paragraph, and the next `\item`, finding `\@inlabel` false, added its own label to the same box (`\hbox_gset:Nn \g__block_labels_box`, which unpacks what's there first): both were set there, the first over the second, "2." over "3.". The PDF's structure had the label in its own item's Lbl all the same. Untagged, `\@labels` holds the label and fancyvrb sets it; LaTeX's own verbatim, as Pandoc sets code in no language, sets each line as a paragraph, which sets the label. Framed's `snugshade`, which item 101 suspected, isn't in it: with the theme's colors Pandoc's `Shaded` is empty. `PDF_MACROS` moves a label waiting in the tagging code's box to `\@labels` before `\FV@ListVSpace` clears `\@inlabel` (`cmd/FV@ListVSpace/before`, added once fancyvrb is loaded), where fancyvrb sets it as it did before the tagging code: only where a label is waiting, so that a fix of LaTeX's own, which would leave none, isn't undone, and nothing without the tagging code. A book's PDF and a deck's take `PDF_MACROS`, and so does the `latex` target's LaTeX (built here with LuaLaTeX, the number in place); a LaTeX book's tagged copy of its own LaTeX (`texremediate.py`) doesn't, and no book here loads fancyvrb. Measured: a bullet's, a nested item's, a quoted list's, and an item's whose code a paragraph follows each set beside the code's first line where the untagged PDF sets it, to a hundredth of a point; a definition that opens with code keeps its term on a line of its own; in a `snugshade`, as a theme with a background would have it, the number set as untagged (a LaTeX file of its own); and veraPDF passing. The PDF suite's margins book and the decks suite's PDF case have such a list, the PDF suite's tagged and untagged, each failing without the change ("Itemopens = 1", "1.2.The item after the code."). Not in the tagging project's issue on fancyvrb (latex3/tagging-project #741, which lists four other problems), so it may be worth reporting there: a LaTeX file of a dozen lines shows it. `formats.md`'s paragraphs on what the run does for LaTeX's tagging, `testing.md`'s rows for the PDF and decks suites, and a Fixed entry in the CHANGELOG say so.

108. **`code_wrap`: how far a block of code is set smaller before its lines wrap.** Rob (2026-10-29, 00:07), of how far wrapping should reach (item 100's offer): "Would it be simple to create a config option to control when to wrap code blocks? Let `1` mean wrap every too-long line and, e.g., `.75` mean wrap when it won't fit at 75%, etc. Otherwise, I'd say that 75% is a good compromise." Built as he said, 0.75 the default, from 0.5 to 1, a target's setting or the defaults' (`code_wrap`, in a book's PDF, a deck's, and the `latex` target's LaTeX): a block of code too wide for its line is set as small as its longest line takes, but no smaller than that part of its size, with the fit's room of 2 percent where there's room for it; a block whose longest line doesn't fit its line even at that part, by the measure's tolerance of half a point, is set at it, and each of its lines too long for its line wraps where it reaches the line's end (item 100). So no code runs into the margin: a block too long for its line at three quarters had run on into it, and one that would have come within a quarter inch of the paper's edge had been set smaller still, to half its size (item 91), only one too long for the paper even at half being wrapped. 1 wraps every line too long for its line at the code's own size.

**How.** The schema gives a number a `minimum` and a `maximum`, outside which `oerconfig` refuses a value, as it refuses a word an enum doesn't have ("should be a number from 0.5 to 1, not 0.3"), and the settings page gives the range. `build-pdf.py` and `decks.build_pdf` write `\def\OERFitCodeWrap{…}` (`latexbuild.code_wrap_latex`) before the fit's macros, which provide it at 0.75 for LaTeX written without it, and `oerfit.next`'s rule for a block of code reads it (`codewrap()`). Built first with the fit's room in the test of whether a block fits, a line of 86 characters, which fits at three quarters (464.4 points of 469.8), wrapped for the want of that room; the test is the line and its tolerance now, and the room is left where there's room for it. `fit_report` says "9 block(s) of code with a line too long for its line even at 75% of their size are set at 75%, each line too long for its line wrapped where it reaches the line's end", or, at the code's own size, "have each such line wrapped".

**Measured.** The PDF suite's code book, where 9 blocks wrap in Plex Mono and 7 in Latin Modern Mono, which holds more to a line; its margins book, where 3 do; and a book of four lines built at 0.75, 1, and 0.5, the lines fitting at 85, 75, 60, and 40 percent of their size, each set whole or wrapped as the setting says, the build saying so; and the decks suite's wide deck at 1, its slide's code wrapped at its own size, where at 0.75 it's set at three quarters and wrapped. By a count of their lines' characters against the text's full line, 44 of OpenStax's 667 blocks of code are wrapped at 0.75, where 7 were: 37 of *Principles of Data Science*'s, 4 of *Introduction to Python Programming*'s, 2 of *Principles of Finance*'s, and 1 of *Foundations of Information Systems*'s; 119 have a line too long for the text at full size, which 1 would wrap (`r31/scripts/code_census31.py`, Round 26's census with the new limits). `formats.md`'s paragraph on code, `configuration.md`'s, the settings page, `testing.md`'s rows, and the CHANGELOG's entry on code say so.

109. **An arrow before each later part of a wrapped line, which no copy holds and no screen reader reads.** Rob (2026-10-29, 00:07), of item 100's offer of a mark at a break: "Can we add an arrow for a wrapped line in such a way that it wouldn't get read and also wouldn't get included in a copy/paste of the code? If not, let's not add it." 111. **Inline code in no language breaks, and a cell's code or table has its room, in a PDF.** Two of the gaps Round 30 left (Open questions), which needed no decision, as Rob said (2026-10-29): "Go ahead and tackle any of the other gaps that you can without a decision needed from me or additional resources." **`\texttt`**, the writer's for inline code in no language, broke only at its spaces, each a `\ `, so a word of it longer than its line ran into the margin (item 105). `pdf-target.lua` puts each span of inline code in a group with `\OERInlineCode`, which marks what it holds, and `oer.inline.code` adds a highlighted span's places to break to a run of glyphs so marked: after a run of spaces, in a word after a run of marks, and between letters only in a word longer than its line. 115. **What the review of Round 31 found.** A separate agent read the round's changes against `main` and built small books for each case it thought of (`r31/rv`): `code_wrap` at its bounds and between them, in Plex Mono and in Latin Modern Mono's designs, on a page of two columns, in a deck, numbered, and untagged; the arrows, tagged and not, copied with `pdftotext`, pypdf, and MuPDF, and veraPDF's PDF/UA-2 profile; the AAA page's measure in Plex and in Latin Modern; `\texttt`'s breaks in a link, a caption, a footnote, an item, a quotation, a heading, struck text, and a definition's term; and tables holding tables three deep. It found those as items 108 to 113 say, and one fault of some weight and six small ones. **Fixed**, each with a check that fails without it: the AAA measure counted a line a line break ends as full, and Pandoc's writer sets a line block's lines and a `LineBreak` as `\\` in one paragraph, so a poem's four short lines among 42 full ones took Latin Modern's average from 83 to 79, and the warning with it; a line that holds glue of infinite stretch isn't counted now (LATEX-NOTES, Line breaking and fitting; the AAA book's poem of 30 lines, and a paragraph of LaTeX's own in the LaTeX suite). A ligature a hyphenation point divides (of-fi-cial) is in the discretionary's `replace` list, which the measure's walk of a line passed over, 19 of 80 characters in a line of such words; it's counted now (the LaTeX suite's paragraph: 7 lines of 638 characters, the PDF's text's, where 447 had been counted). `nested_width` counted a cell across columns as nothing, so a table holding a table whose head is a row across its columns, wider than they are, ran 46 points into each margin at 66 percent of its size; the columns a cell spans are widened to hold it (the fit book). A block of code inside a division in a cell counted as nothing, `cell_size` taking only the cell's own blocks; it walks the cell's blocks for code now (the code book). The `latex` target read back as a LaTeX source put every inline code in a span, the reader making the PDF target's group around it one (`mark_code`, item 111; PANDOC-NOTES, The LaTeX reader); `latexsource.inline_code_marks` takes the group out, as `fit_marks` takes out the fit's (the LaTeX suite's `latex` target, its inline code highlighted and not). `lone_code` lost the code's own id, which a link may name, the paragraph's language, and text after a comment in the paragraph: the code's id is the block's, and the paragraph's then a division's around it, since Pandoc's HTML reader keeps no id of a `pre`'s `code` where the `pre` has one of its own (PANDOC-NOTES, The HTML reader); the paragraph's language is the block's; and a paragraph with text after a comment stays a paragraph (the CNX suite). Its class isn't kept, as Pandoc's reader keeps no paragraph's. None of OpenStax's paragraphs of code alone has any of these: all 7 are *Introduction to Python Programming*'s, each with an id and nothing else. And where a book named Latin Modern Roman for its text and TeX lacked Plex Mono, the fallback's warning, of the monospaced type alone, said the text's lines then missed the criterion, and the measure's own warning was left out: the fallback's warning speaks of the criterion only where the text's face fell back, and the measure's warning is given otherwise (`build-pdf.py`'s `faces_said`, the unit suite). **Its smaller notes, done:** `code_wrap: .nan`, a float no comparison refuses, passed its bounds and became 0.5, and is refused now, as `.inf` is (`oerconfig`, the config suite's fixture 33); the schema says a LaTeX book's PDF built from its own files isn't fitted, so `code_wrap` changes nothing there; `formats.md` says a row with room for fewer than about 22 characters has no arrow, its later parts indented less than two characters; and two comments in `latexbuild.py` that named `\OERInlineCode` for `\VERB`'s box, which `\OERInlineCodeBox` marks, say what each marks now. **The mutations:** 28 of the round's changes, each undone in a copy of the work (`r31/scripts/mutate31.py`), one of them checked on two books; each is caught by a check of the suites but one, the arrow's tagging attributes unset, which changed nothing: a node made in Lua has none, and that code is gone (item 109). 119. **A paragraph of code line by line hangs a wrapped line's later parts on the line.** Rob (2026-10-29, 20:01), of item 105's open question: "Go ahead and implement the solution for the hanging indent that gives the cleanest, most-accessible results. From your description, I think that's the lua pass." *Introduction to Python Programming* sets the output of `help()` (7.4) and a summary in 1.9 as paragraphs of code line by line, every character code and each line ended by a line break (item 112), and a line too long for the text wrapped with its later parts at the margin, as if each were a line of its own. `FIT_MACROS`' `oer.inline.code` now finds such a paragraph's lines and gives each a hang: each part after the first is set the line's indentation and two characters further in, the arrow before it (item 109), as a block's wrapped line is; a line indented so deep that a part would have room for fewer than 20 characters has its parts start 20 characters from the text's edge (`lines_of`); and `oer.code.lines`, in `post_linebreak_filter`, keeps a line's rows on one page unless they'd take more than half of it. The Lua pass Rob chose isn't a second breaking: each place such a line may break is a discretionary break whose text after it is a box as wide as the hang, the arrow drawn at its end (`hang_lines`, `hanger`), so TeX measures each row with it and breaks the paragraph once, where it would; a paragraph shape made from a first breaking, tried first, moved the ragged paragraph's breaks. Three things a first version got wrong, each with a check: a break after a run of spaces in no language kept the spaces at the row's end and counted their width, which moved a row's last word to the next (1.9's summary), and the break's text before it is a kern of minus their width now; the break took the spaces' attributes, which LuaTeX gives the row's right skip, and tagpdf wrote a space for it, two in the structure's text at each break, so it takes the line's first glyph's; and code in no language, whose no-break spaces the writer sets as `~`, lost its indentation at a row's start, TeX dropping glue there after a line break, where an empty box now opens each line (LATEX-NOTES, LuaTeX). **Measured**: *Introduction to Python Programming* built whole, with `main` (2a3f579) and with the change: 376 pages either way and the same 69 fits, and its text, by `pdftotext`, differs only at 1.9's summary, one line's second row, and 7.4's help output, five lines' later rows, each hung where it had started at the margin. The round's review (item 127) found a table's cell of such lines unhung: Pandoc's writer sets a cell that has line breaks ragged right in a `minipage`, where `\\` ends the paragraph (`\@centercr`), so each line was a paragraph of its own and `code_lines` found no line break. A paragraph every character of which is code is hung now, its one line or its lines, so a cell's lines are. Built whole again with the round's final code, *Introduction to Python Programming* differs from the build before the review's fixes on 17 pages, by two of them alone: a table's cell of code wrapped with its later parts hung (chapter 1's table of `print()`'s arguments, one in 9.5, and the summaries of chapters 4, 14, and 15), 14.3's CSV text, one line of code, its later rows hung, and tables whose cells hold inline code given its width (item 123). **Check**: the PDF suite's code book has such a paragraph highlighted and in no language (`LINES_CODE`), and a table's cell of such lines, each kind (`LINES_CELL`), whose hang and arrows it checks too, each line in a part of it: indented two characters, four, 30 with a word of 45, 60, whose parts are capped at 20 characters from the edge, and a line of words that fill a row in Plex Mono but for the space after them; and the paragraph's first lines again at a page's foot. Five checks: the hang and its arrow, with the cap; the indentation; the structure's text; the rows kept on a page; and the full row. Seven mutations, the change undone and each of its parts and faults undone in turn (the tie, the cap's room, the empty box, the break before a line's text, the attributes, the kern), each failed one or more; an eighth, a finite right skip and no demerits for the hang's breaks, failed none, and that code was taken out. Found doing it, and not fixed: a line break leaves no space between its lines in a tagged PDF's text (LATEX-NOTES, Paragraphs and sections).

120. **A formula LaTeX sets as an array is measured without its outer padding: what *College Algebra 2e*'s Example 12 (e) was.** Rob (2026-10-29, 20:01), of Round 32's report that the example fit, where Round 31's had found it 0.6 points too wide: "Let's try to figure out what's happening, in case it's a bug that causes bigger problems later." Both were right, and Round 32's "closed" was wrong. texmath writes an `mtable` whose cells aren't all centered as LaTeX's `array` (PANDOC-NOTES, the HTML reader), Example 12 (e)'s solution as `\begin{array}{ccl}`, and `array` sets the space between two columns, 5 points, blank before the first column and after the last, where amsmath's matrices take it back (LATEX-NOTES, Math). `FIT_MACROS` measured the box, padding and all: at three quarters of its size, the example's box was 0.6 points wider than its line, which Round 31 read from the fit, and its ink ended 1.4 points inside the line, which Round 32 read from the page with `pdftotext`; the fit reported it too wide, and a formula as wide as its line less the padding was set smaller than it needed to be. Nothing had changed between the rounds. `pdf-target.lua`'s `unpadded` writes `@{}` at each edge of such an array with no rule there, but for one right after a delimiter, which the padding keeps off its cells, inside `\left` and `\right` or after one alone, and one inside another's cell. The review (item 127) found the delimiter alone: texmath writes an `mtable` between delimiters MathML says don't stretch (`stretchy="false"`) as `\lbrack\begin{array}{cl}…\end{array}\rbrack`, not inside `\left` and `\right` (measured, Pandoc 3.13, PANDOC-NOTES), and the first version unpadded it, its cells against the brackets. **Measured**: built with the round's final code, *College Algebra 2e*'s section 1.2: in Latin Modern Math, where TeX lacks Noto Sans Math 3.000, Example 12 (e) is set at three quarters of its size, its ink 3.4 points inside the line, and isn't reported too wide, where it was reported 0.6 points too wide; in Noto Sans Math 3.000 it's at its own size, its ink 4.2 points inside the line (LATEX-NOTES, Fonts). **Check**: the PDF suite's fit book has an array between delimiters (`Arraydelimited`) and one after a delimiter alone (`Arrayplain`), its LaTeX checked to keep the padding there and to have none on a bare one (`Arraysmaller`); and the two-column book's worked example too wide for its column even at three quarters of its size, set smaller still, now ends inside the column, where it ran a few points past it and was warned of, one warning of such things where there were two. 165. **The exercise bank in a normal conversion.** Rob's questions (item 163): no step of its own, and not in `convert.py`. `unpack-cnx.py` fetches each exercise a book embeds as it puts the book together, eight at a time, from the bank's public API, and keeps each in its cache (`~/.cache/textbookimprover/cnx-exercises`, `--exercises-cache` naming another); the pages it writes hold the exercises, so `convert.py` never asks the bank for anything, and a book converted again, or to other formats, fetches nothing. An exercise in the cache isn't fetched again, so the cache isn't brought up to date; without the network, one the cache doesn't have is a sentence saying so (`exercise-missing`), and unpacking again with the network, into a new folder, puts it in. A machine that can't reach the bank unpacks from a cache copied to it, with `--offline`. `fetch-exercises.py` (Round 30), which fetched the cache Rob sent without the books' repositories, was for this container, which can't reach the bank, and stays outside the repository. `docs/cnx-input.md` says this now, at the top and under its exercise bank's heading.

168. **A smaller PDF: what there was, what a PDF's bytes are, and `images.compress`'s three levels.** There was `images.downsample` (from the work on LibreTexts' *Instrumental Analysis*, PROJECT-NOTES), a number, the most times an image may be as wide as it's shown, 0 by default, and the run's warning naming it, which *Marketing*'s run printed ("225 image(s) are wider in pixels than the pages show them ... 59.3 MB in all"). **What a PDF's bytes are**: of *Marketing*'s 61.3 MB, 55.8 MB is its images (r42's `scripts/pdfparts.py`): the 110 JPEGs as their files are, 47.9 MB, and the 118 PNGs, each with an alpha channel, 7.9 MB, the rest its fonts, text, and structure. Its structure is in object streams already, so rewriting the file without loss finds nothing: pikepdf's save generating object streams made it 61.27 MB, and compressing its Flate streams again 62.36, larger (LATEX-NOTES, LuaTeX). So a smaller PDF is smaller images. **The JPEGs are the waste**: OpenStax saved 87 of the 110 at quality 99, the most JPEG has but 100, and 21, the chapter openers, at 94 (each JPEG's quality as ImageMagick reports it, and as `jpeg_quality` reads it from the file's luminance table, the same for 109 and one less for the other), all at full color resolution (4:4:4). Written again at their own size, as the run writes them, the 110 are 22.9 MB at quality 90 keeping their color's resolution, 18.0 at half of it (4:2:0, libjpeg's default), and 14.3 at 85 (r42's `scripts/requal42.py`, with the run's own `scale_one`; `sizes42.py`, which didn't write them quite as the run does, had 22.2, 17.3, and 13.6), where scaling every image to twice the width it's shown at, at quality 90, as `images.downsample: 2` does, leaves 49.4 MB of the 59.6, since most of the photographs are no more than 1.4 times as wide as they're shown (`sizes42.py` and `sizes42b.py`). **`images.compress`**, as Rob asked ("design something with a few levels"): `print`, `screen`, or `small`, each a limit, as `images.downsample`'s, which it gives instead when it's set, and the highest quality a JPEG keeps, a JPEG saved at a higher one written again at it, at its own size where it isn't scaled, as is a scaled JPEG: `print` 4 times and quality 90, keeping the JPEG's color resolution; `screen` 2 times and 85; `small` 1 time and 75. The copies are made as `images.downsample`'s are, for the same targets, in a folder per plan; a copy no smaller than its original isn't used; and the warning at the defaults counts the JPEGs saved at a quality over 90 as well (*Marketing*: 110, up to 99). Measured on *Marketing*'s PDF, built with the round's code at each level (`build-pdf.py`, r42's `mkt/levels`): `print`, 36.3 MB, built in 1,065 s: no image scaled, none being more than 3.4 times as wide as it's shown, and the 110 JPEGs written again at quality 90 at their own size, 47.9 MB to 22.9 (built before the resolution fix below, which changes nothing of `print`'s copies, none of them scaled, but their JFIF headers' density, from none to the 200 pixels an inch their EXIF data has, the same length); `screen`, 23.9 MB, built in 968 s: 87 images scaled to twice the width they're shown at, 64 of them drawings given a palette, and the other 88 JPEGs written again at 85, 56.4 MB to 14.9; `small`, 13.4 MB, built in 957 s: 225 images scaled to the width they're shown at, 115 of them drawings given a palette, and the one JPEG left written again at 75, 59.5 MB to 6.6; veraPDF finding nothing in any of the three, as the output check runs it: PDF/UA-2 with Tagged PDF, and WTPDF 1.0's Accessibility and Reuse profiles, none of 1,728, 1,724, and 1,711 rules failed. **Pixels an inch**: the PDF draws an image its page gives no width at its own size, its pixels over its resolution, up to its line's width, 6.5 inches on the default page, where the pages' column is 6 (`\pandocbounded`; *Marketing*'s 800-pixel photographs of 200 pixels an inch are drawn 4 inches wide, at 200 pixels an inch, and its chapter openers, 1,750 pixels wide, across the line, at 269); so a copy keeps at least 576 / 6.5, 88.6, pixels an inch for each time, 354 at `print`, 177 at `screen`, and 89 at `small`, and the configuration page's and the schema's "each step of 1 keeps at least 96 pixels an inch there", written when the default page was Pandoc's, is 89 now. Measured in the PDFs, each image's drawn width read from the pages' content streams (r42's `scripts/placed.py`): with every image whole, and at `print`, which scales none, the 228 are drawn at 200 pixels an inch (91 of them), 269 (19, the chapter openers), and 300 (118, the PNGs); at `screen`, at 177 to 300, the chapter openers at the fewest; at `small`, at 89 to 300; and each at the width it's drawn at with every image whole. **A JPEG copy drawn smaller than its original, found measuring `small`**: its first build had 1,088 pages where the others had 1,102, and 88 of its 228 images were drawn narrower than with every image whole, the narrowest at 0.48 of its width. 89 of *Marketing*'s 110 JPEGs record their resolution in their EXIF data alone, which Pillow reads as an `IFDRational`, a number but not a `float`, so `scale_one`'s check passed over it and wrote the copy's JFIF header without one; and the copy kept the original's EXIF data, 200 pixels an inch, which LuaTeX and Pandoc's Word writer read before the header: a JPEG whose header says 144 pixels an inch and whose EXIF data says 200 is drawn at 200 by LuaTeX in TeX Live 2026 and by Pandoc 3.12.1 and 3.13 in a Word file, so a photograph 800 pixels wide, drawn 4 inches wide, was drawn 2.88 inches wide at `small`, its copy 576 pixels wide (r42's `t/exif`). At `screen` one image was (6.00 inches to 5.76). `images.downsample` had done the same since it was made, unseen, its measurements having been of bytes. Both are fixed (`_exif_for_copy`, and Pillow's number taken as one): the copy's EXIF resolution scaled with its pixels, as its header's is; the unit suite checks a JPEG of the kind (`check_images_plan`), and each of the fix's three mutations is caught; it does the same with Pillow 10.1.0, tried by hand on that JPEG and one of *Marketing*'s, where every setup here has 12.3.0, and Ubuntu 22.04's 9.0, which `downsample.py` allows for, wasn't tried; and `small` and `screen` were built again with it, as above. **Grayscale**, Rob's question: on top of a level, the images in shades of gray would be 43 percent smaller at `print` (34.6 MB to 19.8, `print` keeping the color's resolution), 25 percent at `screen` (18.1 to 13.5), and 13 percent at `small` (6.6 to 5.8), their files' bytes (r42's `scripts/gray42.py`, run again with the resolution fix above, which made `small`'s copies 0.5 MB smaller, and `screen`'s and `print`'s no smaller at a tenth of one), and the PDF, nearly all images, about as many megabytes smaller, roughly 41, 19, and 6 percent of it: less than the levels themselves save, and it takes away what color says, a chart's series or a map's regions, which a book's text and a reader's eye go by (WCAG's 1.4.1 asks that color not be the only way something is said, which a book's figures don't always meet), so there's no gray level; a reader who prints in black and white gets gray from the printer. **The JPEGs written again**, against their originals: at quality 90, 36.0 dB (PSNR) at the median and 28.3 at worst, MKT_Figure_16_02_006, a photograph of colored words on a textured board, 35.1 when it keeps its color's resolution, as `print` does; at 85 with half the color, 34.9 and 27.7; at 75, 33.5 and 26.6 (r42's `scripts/psnr42.py`). A crop of that photograph at twice its size, side by side at each (`size/look/crops.png`), showed me no difference but a little softness at colored letters' edges at half the color's resolution; and a chapter opener's page rendered at 200 dots an inch, whole and at `screen`, looked the same (`size/look/page24-crops.png`). **Memory**: two of the levels' builds at once, with veraPDF beside them, ran out of the memory the container gives its commands, the kernel killing LuaLaTeX mid-run, whose cut-off `.aux` stopped the next run at `\begin{document}` ("File ended while scanning use of \@newl@bel"), as LATEX-NOTES says it does; each was built again alone.

169. **The exercise cache, brought up to date on request: `--update-exercises`.** The cache isn't brought up to date on its own, which the CNX page said since Round 41 (item 165) and now `unpack-cnx.py`'s docstring and `--help`, `cnx.exercises`' docstring, and the CHANGELOG say too. `--update-exercises` asks the bank again for each exercise the book embeds that the cache has, eight at a time, as a first unpacking asks, and writes the bank's over the cache's copy where it's newer: a later version of an exercise the two share by number, and none earlier, or other exercises (each exercise the bank keeps has a number and a version, `uid` 84@9, and its versions and when it was published); at the same versions the cache's copy stays, whatever else the two answers differ in (item 171, the review's design note). One the cache hasn't is fetched as on a first unpacking. The cache's copy is kept where the bank's is an earlier version, where the bank has none now, or where it can't be asked, each a row of the report (`exercise-not-updated`, with why), and an exercise written over is one too (`exercise-updated`, with both versions); the run counts them. It's refused with `--offline`. **Rob's question, whether comparing files' modification times would do**: no. A file's time in the cache is when it was fetched, and nothing short of asking for an exercise says when the bank's changed: the cache keeps the bank's answer, not the reply's headers, so whether the bank answers a conditional request (`If-Modified-Since`, an `ETag`) isn't known here, and this container can't reach the bank to find out; and once an exercise is asked for, its version is the surer comparison. A picture an exercise shows is fetched by its address and isn't fetched again: an S3 key is the SHA-256 of the picture's bytes (all 283 such keys among the 26 books' exercises, checked against the cached pictures), so a changed picture has a new address, which an updated exercise names and the unpacking fetches; one at the bank's own `active_storage` address names an upload, and is taken to be the same. Tested against a stand-in for the bank, `Bank._fetch` replaced by one that answers from a file (`tests/run-cnx-tests.py`, `BANK_RUNNER`): without the option, an exercise the cache has isn't asked for though the bank's is newer; with it, each is asked for once, a newer one written over the cache's copy and reported, one at the same version left as it is, an earlier one, none, one that can't be asked, and one whose reply is cut off partway keeping the cache's copy, each reported, and one the cache hadn't, fetched, asked once more where its first reply fails, as on a first unpacking; with `--offline`, refused. The bank itself couldn't be reached to try it.

170. **`util/fetch-exercises.py` and `tests/pandoc39/`, in the repository, as Rob asked.** **`fetch-exercises.py`**, Round 30's, which fetched the cache Rob sent for 26 books without their repositories, made a utility: it finds the library beside `util/` rather than taking the folder as an argument; given repositories, it puts each of their books together as `unpack-cnx.py` does (`cnx.exercises.wanted`, the exercises an assembled book embeds, which `inject` uses too), and `--write-list` writes them as the list Round 30's read, without the network; `--list` reads such a list; it fetches the exercises and their pictures into the cache, as unpacking does, `--exercises-cache` and `--update-exercises` taken as `unpack-cnx.py` takes them; `--zip` packs the cache's files for them to carry, an earlier run's zip files in its folder removed first; and what can't be had goes in `fetch-failures.tsv` in the folder it's run from, as does, with `--update-exercises`, an exercise the bank couldn't be asked about again, the run's exit 1, the file removed by a run that has everything. Tested with the bank's stand-in: the list written without the network, fetched, zipped without asking, and a book unpacked offline from the zip's files. The utilities page and the CNX page say how. **The stand-in for Pandoc 3.9** (Round 41's `shim39`) is `tests/pandoc39/`: `pandoc`, `data/init.lua`, and `options-3.9.txt`. It runs the Pandoc `PANDOC39_REAL` names, or else the first on the `PATH` that isn't a stand-in, itself or a copy in another clone, known by the words its docstring opens with, where Round 41's ran `/root/bin/pandoc`; it runs only over 3.11 or later, which has `--math-method`, `--version` saying so otherwise; and it tells the Pandoc it runs how many stand-ins deep it is (`PANDOC39_DEPTH`), one ten deep stopping, saying so (item 171 has why). `run-all.sh`, run with it first on the `PATH`, names the Pandoc it runs in `PANDOC39_REAL` for every suite, and says which: six checks of the convert suite hide the `PATH`'s other programs from a run, to see it stop without LaTeX, say, and keep a link to whatever `pandoc` is, the stand-in, which then found no other Pandoc and stopped, failing them, in the first run of every suite under it (Round 41's `shim39` ran a Pandoc at a fixed path, and so passed); the decks and LaTeX suites hide programs the same way. The testing page says how to run one suite on its own under it. The unit suite checks that it still answers as 3.9, its folder first on the `PATH` as the suites run under it, that a copy after it on the `PATH` is passed over, and that a run ten deep stops; the portability suite reads it; `run-all.sh` and the testing page say how to run under it, and that it's to be run before each release through 1.0, as Rob said ("I'd like to keep the compatibility through TI version 1.0"); and the installation page names it. It's for Linux and macOS, whose `PATH` finds a script by its name.

171. **Round 42's review, and what it found.** A reviewer given the round's work as a commit (5a45d40), not my account of it, found eleven defects, each confirmed by a run, and made a design note; all are fixed. (1) A check I'd added to `Bank.get`, that an exercise whose fetch had failed isn't asked for again, applied in every mode, so a first unpacking no longer asked again for one whose fetch among eight at once had failed, as it had; it's gone, `refresh` keeping its own. (2) The settings page wasn't made again from the schema, which `run-all.sh` checks. (3) A reply cut off partway (`http.client.IncompleteRead`, an `HTTPException`, not an `OSError`) stopped the run with a traceback, in `get` and `image` before this round too; `FETCH_ERRORS` takes it now, and the bank's stand-in answers so for one exercise. (4) The stand-in's unit check took any answer but 3.9's for a reason to skip, so a broken stand-in passed; the skip is decided by the Pandoc it runs now, found as it finds it. (5) `fetch-exercises.py --zip` left an earlier, larger run's parts beside the new, an exercise in both; it removes them. (6) The summary counted an exercise the cache hadn't and the bank couldn't give as fetched; it's counted apart. (7) An earlier run's `fetch-failures.tsv` outlived a run that fetched everything; it's removed. (8) `fetch-exercises.py --update-exercises` exited 0 when the bank couldn't be asked about anything; it exits 1. (9) A JPEG wider than the limit and saved at a quality below the level's was written at the level's, so its copy often came out larger and was kept whole; it's written at its own. (10) `images.downsample: 0` beside a level doesn't keep every image whole, as the schema and configuration page said; they say now that 0 leaves the limit to the level, and that one larger than any image's width over the width it's shown at, 100 say, keeps every image's pixels. (11) The stand-in put `--math-method=plain` after a `--`, where it's a file's name; it goes before the arguments. The design note: `refresh` wrote the bank's answer over the cache's at the same versions where the two differed, so an answer carrying something that changes with each request would make every exercise newer on every run; at the same versions the cache's copy stays now. **Mutations**: 47 mutations of the round's code, each an edit a mistake could make, every one caught by the checks that should catch it (r42's `scripts/mut42.py`): 18 of `images.compress` and the copies it and `images.downsample` make, 13 of `--update-exercises`, 5 of `fetch-exercises.py`, and 11 of the stand-in, among them each review fix and the resolution fix undone. One did more than fail: the stand-in finding itself on the `PATH`, asked its version, asked itself, and so on, a chain of Python processes that outlived the check's time limit, since `subprocess.run` kills only the process it started, until the container's memory ran out and the kernel killed the small level's build with it. A second copy of the repository's stand-in on the `PATH` would have done the same, each running the other, since it passed over only itself. So it passes over any copy of itself now, known by the words its docstring opens with, tells the Pandoc it runs how many stand-ins deep it is (`PANDOC39_DEPTH`), and stops ten deep, saying so; its check covers both, and the mutations of them were caught in seconds. **Suites**: every suite at the code's last commit (tree `7017922`; 1f67c3e as the suites ran it, its hash another in the mailbox), in `313`, Pandoc 3.13 (2,983 s), and `312`, 3.12.1 (1,812 s), and under the stand-in for 3.9 (`pandoc39`, 3.12.1 beneath it, 3,035 s, the PowerPoint and reveal.js targets' checks skipping, as they need 3.10.1 and 3.12), all passing; the unit and CNX suites in the nine other setups (`tiny`, `py312`, `rob2`, `notex`, `bare`, `oldlatex`, `nogs`, `nopikepdf`, `nopoppler`), all passing; and at each of the two commits before it, the unit suite, and the convert suite's case of `images.compress` at the first and the CNX suite at the second, passing (r42's `scripts/steps42.sh`), so that each commit stands on its own. The notes' commit changes nothing but the three notes.
